# FOSS Category Taxonomy & Intelligence Report — 2026-10-12

> **Catalog Source**: `inputs/foss_toolcatalogs/ytgithurepos_20261012.html`  
> **Dataset Scope**: 418 Video Curations · 8,908 Product Instances · 7,880 Deduplicated Repositories  
> **Categorized Working Set**: 4,775 Repositories across 65 Categories  
> **Analysis Date**: October 12, 2026  

## Executive Overview
This report presents an exhaustive deep-and-wide analysis and categorization of the open-source software tools compiled within the October 12, 2026 FOSS catalog. Each repository was analyzed across architectural dimensions, source provenance, license posture, and concrete functionality, mapping them against the authoritative 65-category software spine specified by the system architecture.

All tool descriptions, extended synopses, attached metadata (keywords, tags, topics), star trajectories, and video provenance records were extracted directly from the primary HTML source. In addition, an interactive client-side **FOSS Category Explorer** web application (`index.html`) has been generated in this subfolder, featuring real-time card/table/group rendering, multi-field search, keyword filtering, notes persistence, and export functionality.

## Key Architectural & Strategic Findings

### 1. The Proliferation of Coding Agent Observability & Skills (Cats 04, 34, 44)
The 2026 FOSS ecosystem is dominated by an explosion of agentic developer tooling. Categories 04 (Agent Skills), 34 (Coding Agent Observability), and 44 (Self-Learning Agent Skills) collectively account for over 800 repositories. Projects like `observal`, `optim-plans`, `numbat`, `truedeck`, and `codejury` illustrate the transition from monolithic chat interfaces to modular, skill-based, multi-agent supervisory architectures.

### 2. Modern Web & Desktop Spine: Svelte 5 and Tauri 2 (Cats 50, 51)
Categories 50 (Svelte Frontend UI/UX) and 51 (Desktop Development with Tauri 2) exhibit strong traction, counting 100 and 125 tools respectively. Tauri v2 has emerged as the clear standard for native cross-platform AI workbenches (e.g. `OpenSlides`, `devtools-x`, `pake`), leveraging Rust backends with Svelte 5 runes for high-performance, low-memory footprints compared to traditional Electron apps.

### 3. Real-Time Backends: Postgres, Supabase, and Fastify (Cats 09, 10)
Over 450 projects populate the Postgres and Supabase ecosystems. Modern setups heavily favor TypeScript + Node.js/Fastify for high-throughput APIs (`fastify`, `bun-sqlgen`, `better-drizzle`) coupled with Supabase Realtime and pgvector for low-latency live synchronization and semantic retrieval.

# Android Automation & Device Control — FOSS Tools Intelligence Dossier

> **Catalog Date**: 2026-10-12  
> **Primary Source**: `inputs/foss_toolcatalogs/ytgithurepos_20261012.html`  
> **Interactive App**: [`index.html`](file:///d:/stuff/ai-misc/_bsh2026/vscode_project01/46-wide_research_test_gemini/deliverables/2026-10-12-foss-category-explorer/index.html)  
> **Category Alignment**: Taxonomy Category 12 (*Browser Control / Browser Automation / Android Emulator Control*) & Mobile Agent Ecosystem

## Executive Summary

Within the October 12, 2026 FOSS catalog snapshot, mobile and Android automation represents one of the fastest evolving frontiers. The tooling has evolved significantly beyond conventional headless scrapers and static Appium test suites, branching into **six distinct technical paradigms**:
1. **Autonomous Phone Agents (Vision & GUI-Action Models)**: Multimodal models (Qwen-VL, AutoGLM) that observe raw mobile screens, plan multi-step workflows, and execute autonomous taps, swipes, and text input.
2. **High-Performance Screen Mirroring & Low-Latency Controllers**: Desktop and web applications utilizing `scrcpy` and custom ADB video streams to enable real-time device interaction.
3. **Multi-Device Parallel ADB Automation**: Orchestration layers that broadcast scripted interactions across farm deployments of physical Android devices via ADB.
4. **Model Context Protocol (MCP) Mobile Drivers**: Dedicated MCP servers exposing native Android UI trees, input injection, and screenshot feeds directly to coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.
5. **Virtual Phone & Research Emulator Workstations**: CLI and GUI utilities orchestrating virtualized mobile environments for sandboxed testing and automated security verification.
6. **Rootless System Bridges & APK Reverse Engineering**: Automation tools leveraging Shizuku and agent skill packs to decompile, inspect, and automate apps without requiring root privileges.

## Detailed Tool Profiles by Architectural Cluster

### Autonomous Phone Agents & Vision Controllers

#### 1. [Open-AutoGLM](https://github.com/zai-org/Open-AutoGLM) (`zai-org/Open-AutoGLM`)
- **Repository URL**: [https://github.com/zai-org/Open-AutoGLM](https://github.com/zai-org/Open-AutoGLM)
- **Project Homepage**: [https://autoglm.z.ai/blog](https://autoglm.z.ai/blog)
- **Primary Language**: `Python` | **Stars**: `★ 24,979` | **License**: `Apache-2.0`
- **Video Provenance**: Channel: *ManuAGI - AutoGPT Tutorials* | Video: *Top New Open-Source GitHub Projects This Week: AI, Mobile Agents & Dev Workflows #216* | Date: *2025-12-14*
- **Keywords**: `mobile-development, automation, ai-agents, programming-languages, computer-vision, education`

**Product Description Text**:
> An Open Phone Agent Model & Framework. Unlocking the AI Phone for Everyone

**Detailed Synopsis / Architectural Context**:
> Open-AutoGLM is an open-source framework and model designed to create an intelligent Phone Agent capable of automating mobile tasks. It leverages the AutoGLM model and vision-language capabilities to understand the content of a phone screen and execute complex actions. The system utilizes ADB (Android Debug Bridge) for device control, allowing it to interact with the operating system and perform operations. Users can issue natural language commands, which the agent translates into a sequence of visual perceptions, planning, and physical actions. Key features include built-in sensitive operation confirmation and remote ADB debugging for flexible control. This project aims to unlock the potential of AI for hands-free mobile interaction.


#### 2. [gelab-zero](https://github.com/stepfun-ai/gelab-zero?tab=readme-ov-file#-application-demonstrations) (`stepfun-ai/gelab-zero`)
- **Repository URL**: [https://github.com/stepfun-ai/gelab-zero?tab=readme-ov-file#-application-demonstrations](https://github.com/stepfun-ai/gelab-zero?tab=readme-ov-file#-application-demonstrations)
- **Project Homepage**: [https://opengelab.github.io/](https://opengelab.github.io/)
- **Primary Language**: `Python` | **Stars**: `★ 2,254` | **License**: `MIT`
- **Video Provenance**: Channel: *Cooly* | Video: *Cooly's Chrome Links* | Date: *2026-09-02*
- **Keywords**: `automation, benchmark, python, agent, mcp, android, framework`
- **Topics**: `agent, gui-agents, phone-use-agent, pua`

**Product Description Text**:
> GELab: GUI Exploration Lab. One of the best GUI agent solutions in the galaxy, built by the StepFun-GELab team and powered by Step’s research capabilities.

**Detailed Synopsis / Architectural Context**:
> GELab-Zero addresses the fragmented engineering challenges of deploying GUI-based mobile agents by providing a fully open-source, plug-and-play solution with both model and infrastructure. It combines a lightweight 4B GUI agent model—capable of running locally on consumer hardware for low latency and privacy—with a complete inference engineering pipeline that handles multi-device ADB management, dependency setup, task distribution, and interaction recording. The system supports three agent working modes (ReAct loops, multi-agent collaboration, and scheduled tasks), offers MCP server integration for multi-device coordination, and ships with the AndroidDaily benchmark for evaluating real-world mobile tasks. Developed by the StepFun-GELab team, it targets Agent developers seeking rapid testing of new strategies and enterprise users looking to integrate MCP capabilities without rebuilding infrastructure from scratch. Practical demonstrations span recommendations, metro queries, welfare claims, and complex multi-item grocery shopping across diverse apps and device brands.

**Product Description Text**:
> Android Phone Control With Qwen3-VL

**Detailed Synopsis / Architectural Context**:
> The Phone Driver is a Python-based mobile automation agent designed for controlling Android devices through visual and natural language interaction. It leverages the Qwen3-VL vision-language model to visually analyze phone screens and understand user intent. The agent integrates these visual insights with ADB commands to plan and execute complex mobile tasks. Key features include real-time feedback, a Gradio web interface for control, and the ability to process commands in plain English. By combining visual analysis with ADB integration, the system automates actions such as opening apps or changing settings on the device. This repository provides a framework for advanced, vision-powered mobile automation.


#### 4. [droidclaw](https://github.com/unitedbyai/droidclaw) (`unitedbyai/droidclaw`)

- **Keywords**: `mobile-development, automation, ai-agents, programming-languages, education`

**Product Description Text**:
> turn old phones into ai agents - give it a goal in plain english. it reads the screen, thinks about what to do, taps and types via adb, and repeats until the job is done.

**Detailed Synopsis / Architectural Context**:
> Droidclaw is an AI agent designed to transform Android phones into functional agents capable of executing complex tasks. It operates by implementing a perception-reasoning-action loop, allowing the agent to read the screen, understand the context, and decide the next physical action. The system uses ADB commands to interact with the device, performing taps, typing, and navigation based on a plain English goal provided by the user. At its core, it leverages a Large Language Model (LLM) to process visual input and generate logical plans for execution. **Detailed Synopsis / Architectural Context**:
> apk-reverse is an Agent Skill (for Claude Code, Codex, and compatible harnesses) that performs Android APK reverse engineering, debloating, ad removal, dex-level patching, and runtime/server protocol analysis. It targets the recurring failure mode where AI models read instructions, agree with them, and then revert to first-principles reasoning, replacing open-ended advice with a procedural framework of four override rules (R1–R4), four verification gates (G1–G4), a symptom-index-driven stop-signal catalog, and a two-strike rule to prevent repeated identical mistakes. The skill distinguishes client-side feasibility from server-enforced paywalls, selects the safest patch layer for a given change, and catches silent failures such as repacked APKs whose signed requests are rejected because the signing key is derived from the original certificate. It is packaged for progressive disclosure, with a short decision-oriented `SKILL.md`, on-demand reference files (e.g. `advanced-unpacking.md`), parameterized Python scripts such as `doctor.py` for environment diagnosis, and Markdown coverage, with a Python Markdown Markdown Android toolchain spanning MT Manager, LSPosed, Frida (including Stalker and RPC service-ification), and OLLVM-flattened native analysis, aimed at security researchers, reverse engineers, and developers debugging or hardening Android applications.

**Detailed Synopsis / Architectural Context**:
> Teardroid v4 is an educational Android botnet toolkit that simplifies building a remote access trojan (RAT) without requiring port forwarding, a VPS, or Android Studio. It provides a Python-based builder that generates a customized APK payload, paired with a web-based control panel deployable on Deta.sh for remote command execution. The tool enables operators to extract contacts, SMS, call logs, device location, and installed apps, as well as run shell commands, change wallpapers, send SMS, make calls, read notifications, and download files from compromised devices. Security researchers, penetration testers, and students studying Android malware use it to understand mobile threat vectors in controlled, authorized environments. The stack combines Python 3 for the builder and API, Java (JDK 11) for APK construction, and Deta Cloud microservices for hosting the admin dashboard, supporting Linux and Windows hosts. A disclaimer explicitly states the tool is for educational purposes only, with the author disclaiming responsibility for any malicious use.

> Rootless wifi-tethering bypass for Android with Shizuku.

**Detailed Synopsis / Architectural Context**:
> Shizzi enables unlimited Wi-Fi tethering on Android devices by routing hotspot traffic through a test TUN interface using Shizuku's elevated privileges, bypassing carrier hotspot data caps. It creates a test network, configures it as the preferred tethering upstream, and forwards traffic via a Go-based datapath with support for both IPv4 and IPv6. The app requires Android 11 or higher on arm64 devices with Shizuku 13.6.0+, and on Android 11/12 it may prompt users to install a compatibility module for the device's tethering stack. Key features include VPN compatibility for per-device privacy, integration with the existing Android hotspot (no extra setup), a quick settings tile for one-tap control, and automation support via Tasker or MacroDroid. Built with Go (compiled to native bindings via gomobile) and Android SDK/NDK, it delivers this functionality without requiring root access, making it ideal for mobile users seeking to share their regular mobile data allowance over Wi-Fi tethering.

## Strategic Analysis: The Future of Android Automation

### 1. The Transition from Selector-Based Testing to Visual Phone Agents
Traditional Android automation relied on fragile accessibility node trees (XPath, resource IDs) that broke across OEM skins (OneUI, MIUI, Pixel UI). The emergence of **Open-AutoGLM**, **PhoneDriver**, and **gelab-zero** marks a transition toward multimodal vision-language models that process direct framebuffer screenshots and emit standardized coordinate touch gestures (`click(x, y)`, `scroll(dir)`).

### 2. Standardizing Agent Access via Model Context Protocol (MCP)
With projects like **mobile-mcp** and **qapilot-mcp-for-android**, developers can now expose mobile devices as first-class tools in IDEs (Claude Code, Cursor). An agent can autonomously run an Android app, observe visual layout glitches, inspect logcat streams via ADB, and commit bug fixes in a closed feedback loop.

### 3. Lightweight Hardware Farming
Tools like **droidclaw** and **Social-Media-Automation** highlight a growing trend: repurposing inexpensive or decommissioned Android devices into dedicated, always-on AI automation nodes connected over Wi-Fi or USB.

# Browser Automation, Web Scraping, Headless Runtimes & Data Harvesting — FOSS Intelligence Dossier

> **Catalog Snapshot Date**: October 12, 2026  
> **Primary Dataset**: `inputs/foss_toolcatalogs/ytgithurepos_20261012.html` (7,880 Repositories, 65 Categories)  
> **Featured External Inclusion**: [`webbrain-one/webbrain`](https://github.com/webbrain-one/webbrain) (AI Browser Agent Monorepo)  
> **Interactive App**: [`index.html`](file:///d:/stuff/ai-misc/_bsh2026/vscode_project01/46-wide_research_test_gemini/deliverables/2026-10-12-foss-category-explorer/index.html)  
> **Primary Category Cross-Reference**: Category 12 (*Browser Control / Browser Automation*), Category 61 (*Web Scraping / Data Extraction*), Category 57 (*Text Extraction*), Category 08 (*Automation Workflows*)  

## Executive Summary

Within the modern open-source software landscape captured in the October 2026 catalog, browser automation, web data extraction, and headless interaction tooling have undergone a fundamental paradigm shift. Where legacy automation relied upon rigid CSS/XPath locators and brittle WebDriver bindings, modern 2026 engineering has converged around **four foundational technical pillars**:

1. **Autonomous AI Browser Agents & Side-Panel Navigators**: Autonomous agents that perceive live web pages via visual embeddings, accessibility trees, and DOM snapshots. Exemplified by [`webbrain-one/webbrain`](https://github.com/webbrain-one/webbrain) and `browser-use/browser-use`, these tools execute high-level intent ("book a flight", "extract pricing tiers", "navigate multi-factor flows") by interleaving planning with real-time DOM action loops.
2. **Headless Browser Engines, Stealth Runtimes & Native CDP Controllers**: Tooling designed to bypass increasingly aggressive bot detection systems (Cloudflare Turnstile, DataDome, Akamai). Engines like `CloakHQ/CloakBrowser` patch V8 runtime leaks and WebGL/Canvas fingerprints, while lightweight runtimes like `lightpanda-io/browser` (written in native Zig) and `autoscrape-labs/pydoll` interface directly with Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) without heavy WebDriver overhead.
3. **Web Scraping & High-Performance Crawling Frameworks**: High-throughput frameworks engineered to transform unstructured web pages into clean, token-efficient Markdown and JSON. Powerhouses like `firecrawl/firecrawl` (158k★) and `unclecode/crawl4ai` (78k★) serve as the ingestion engines for modern RAG pipelines and LLM training sets.
4. **Data Harvesting, DOM/Article Text Extraction & Document Pipelines**: Specialized heuristic and ML-based extractors (such as `adbar/trafilatura`, `AndyTheFactory/newspaper4k`, and `docling-project/docling`) that discard boilerplate navigation, cookie banners, and ads to extract pure prose, semantic tables, and structured article metadata.

## Featured Architecture Spotlight: WebBrain (`webbrain-one/webbrain`)

At the explicit request of the research brief, [`webbrain-one/webbrain`](https://github.com/webbrain-one/webbrain) has been integrated into this intelligence dossier as the prime case study of modern **in-browser agentic architecture**.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         WEBBRAIN AGENT ARCHITECTURE                         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┤
│           ACTIVE BROWSER TABS           │      WEBBRAIN SIDE-PANEL EXT      │
│                                         │                                   │
│  ┌────────────┐   ┌──────────────────┐  │  ┌─────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ DOM Tree   │   │ Network Traffic  │  │  │ Ask Mode (Read & Extract)   │  │
│  ├────────────┤   ├──────────────────┤  │  ├─────────────────────────────┤  │
│  │ Page Visual│   │ Console Logs     │  │  │ Act Mode (Click, Type, Form)│  │
│  └─────┬──────┘   └─────────┬────────┘  │  ├─────────────────────────────┤  │
│        │                    │           │  │ Dev Mode (CSS, DOM Mutate)  │  │
│        └─────────┬──────────┘           │  └──────────────┬──────────────┘  │
│                  │ Live Event Bridge    │                 │                 │
│                  ▼                      │                 │                 │
│         Chrome / Firefox APIs           │                 │ Orchestration   │
│         (Manifest V3 / Scripting) ◄─────┴─────────────────┘                 │
└──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                           │ Model Execution Loop (Local & Cloud)
                           ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┐
│            LOCAL LLM RUNTIMES           │          FRONTIER CLOUD APIs      │
│  • Ollama (:11434/v1)                   │  • OpenAI (GPT-4o, o1, o3)        │
│  • llama.cpp / llama-server (:8080)     │  • Anthropic Claude 3.5/3.7       │
│  • vLLM (:8000/v1)                      │  • Google Gemini 2.0 / 2.5        │
│  • LM Studio / Jan / LocalAI / Osaurus  │  • DeepSeek V3 / R1               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Key Architectural Attributes of WebBrain:
- **Cross-Browser Monorepo**: Engineered with native manifests for Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, and Microsoft Edge, deployable unpacked from source or pre-built via `npm run build:chrome` and `npm run build:firefox`.
- **Three Tri-Modal Operating Personas**:
  1. **Ask Mode (Read-Only Comprehension)**: Safe read-only inspection for answering questions about active pages, locating target links, extracting data, and synthesizing summaries without state mutation.
  2. **Act Mode (Autonomous Agent)**: Interactive execution engine that plans and invokes synthetic clicks, keyboard text input, multi-hop navigation, form submission, and file downloads.
  3. **Dev Mode (Technical Inspector)**: Full developer telemetry access exposing raw page HTML source, computed CSS styles, runtime console errors, network traffic waterfalls, and reversible live DOM patches.
- **Privacy-First Local LLM Support**: Native loopback adapters for Ollama, llama-server, vLLM, LM Studio, Osaurus, and CLIProxyAPI, enabling zero-data-leakage browser automation on air-gapped consumer hardware.
- **Dynamic Context Compaction**: Automatically queries server metadata (context capacity) before attaching heavy base64 screenshots, progressively compressing conversation history as the context window approaches saturation.

**Detailed Synopsis / Architectural Context**:
> WebBrain is an open-source browser extension monorepo (supporting Chrome, Firefox, and Microsoft Edge) that embeds an autonomous AI agent directly into the browser side panel. It allows users and autonomous workflows to chat with active web pages, execute multi-step automation tasks, extract structured content, and interact with the live DOM. The extension supports local model execution (Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM, LM Studio, Jan, LocalAI) as well as commercial cloud APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, DeepSeek, Mistral). WebBrain introduces three foundational operational modes: Ask (read-only comprehension, page summarization, link finding), Act (autonomous action execution: clicking, typing, navigating, form completion, and file downloading), and Dev (deep technical inspection: DOM tree source, CSS styles, console logs, network telemetry, and reversible page modifications). It features dynamic context-window sizing, server metadata extraction before screenshot injection, and hot-swappable local LLM backends.

> MCP server turning Xiaohongshu, Douyin, TikTok, YouTube or WeChat links into text with a read receipt; skills for Claude Code and Cursor. GH: 2★, pushed 2026-10-08.

**Detailed Synopsis / Architectural Context**:
> LinkDigest MCP is an AI-agent skill that converts social media links from platforms like Xiaohongshu (小红书), Douyin (抖音), TikTok, YouTube, and WeChat into structured, machine-readable text. It addresses the challenge that platforms return tokenized share URLs, app shells, or login walls rather than actual post content, extracting transcripts, on-screen text (OCR), image descriptions, captions, and metadata. The hosted service is exposed as a remote MCP server over streamable HTTP at `https://linkdigest.dev/mcp`, with the repository also providing a Python-based stdio bridge, a zero-dependency Python SDK, and a `linkdigest` command-line interface.

Key features include a single `digest_url` tool that returns structured markdown or JSON output, optional viral breakdowns with quotes verified against source content, translations, and targeted question-answering grounded in post text. The repository ships with eleven ready-to-use agent skills covering specific use cases like Xiaohongshu OCR, video transcription, and script rewriting, each implemented as a `SKILL.md` plus a Python standard-library-only script. It integrates with Claude Code, Cursor, OpenClaw, Hermes, Dify, and any stdio-only MCP client via `mcp-remote`, with a free one-summary-per-day tier and 10 sign-up credits requiring no payment card.

The technology stack combines a hosted reading engine (closed source) accessed over HTTPS with open-source MIT-licensed components: a Python SDK, a Dify plugin, Cursor plugin conf


---

## Strategic Engineering Synthesis & Architectural Trends

### 1. The Death of Brittle Locators: The Shift to Visual Grounding & Agentic Loops
For over two decades, browser automation was dominated by deterministic DOM querying using CSS selectors and XPath expressions. However, modern dynamic single-page applications (SPAs) featuring obfuscated CSS modules, shadow DOMs, canvas renderings, and randomized class names cause deterministic scripts to break frequently. The tools highlighted in this dossier showcase the modern solution: **visual grounding coupled with accessibility-tree abstraction**.
- Systems such as `browser-use/browser-use`, `Skyvern-AI/Skyvern`, and `browserbase/stagehand` feed multimodal screenshots and semantic tree nodes into LLMs, enabling the agent to identify interactive targets based on semantic intent rather than brittle DOM paths.
- Extensions like `webbrain-one/webbrain` execute this loop directly in the user's live browser instance, eliminating the need to set up remote browser farms for daily productivity tasks.

### 2. The Anti-Bot Arms Race: Stealth Chromium & Direct CDP Injection
Modern web scraping faces sophisticated bot mitigation vendors (Cloudflare Turnstile, DataDome, Kasada, PerimeterX) that analyze TLS fingerprints, JavaScript execution speed, canvas noise, and navigator property leaks.
- Standard automation tools like vanilla Puppeteer or Selenium fail instant detection tests because `window.navigator.webdriver = true` and CDP artifacts are exposed.
- Projects like `CloakHQ/CloakBrowser` (27.2k★), `vinyzu-archive/botright`, and `jo-inc/camofox-browser` patch the Chromium source code directly to randomize hardware telemetry and mimic organic human touch/mouse bezier curves.
- Simultaneously, libraries like `autoscrape-labs/pydoll` bypass WebDriver entirely by communicating directly over asynchronous WebSockets to the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), drastically reducing memory footprint and avoiding standard automation flags.

### 3. Native Lightweight Runtimes: The Emergence of Lightpanda and Servo
Running full-fledged Chromium headless instances incurs massive memory and CPU overhead (often 300MB–1GB RAM per active browser tab). In high-volume data harvesting and crawler operations, this creates severe scaling bottlenecks.
- `lightpanda-io/browser` represents a breakthrough architecture: a headless browser engine built from scratch in **Zig** designed specifically for AI agents, crawlers, and scrapers. By focusing purely on execution of JavaScript and DOM evaluation without layout rendering pipelines, it achieves sub-10ms startup times and a fraction of Chromium's RAM footprint.
- `servo/servo` continues to evolve in Rust, delivering parallel layout computation and modular engine embedding for high-performance content consumption.

### 4. Convergence of Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Browser Control
A major pattern emerging in the 2026 ecosystem is the standardization of browser automation tools into Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. Rather than hardcoding custom Python or TypeScript automation scripts into AI agents:
- `ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp` (48.2k★) and `microsoft/playwright-mcp` (31.0k★) expose standardized tool interfaces (`navigate`, `click`, `take_screenshot`, `evaluate_script`, `get_console_logs`) directly to coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.
- Stealth variations like `feder-cr/invisible_playwright_mcp` allow agents to conduct deep intelligence gathering and autonomous navigation while remaining undetected by anti-bot firewalls.

### 5. Structured LLM-Native Ingestion Pipelines
Traditional web scrapers output raw HTML, leaving downstream applications with megabytes of noisy markup containing script tags, tracker beacons, and inline styles. The state-of-the-art tools featured here (`firecrawl/firecrawl`, `unclecode/crawl4ai`, `adbar/trafilatura`, `docling-project/docling`):
- Automatically strip headers, footers, modal overlays, and advertisements.
- Convert tabular HTML into clean Markdown tables or typed Pydantic models.
- Calculate readability metrics to yield token-minimized, high-density text optimized for context-constrained LLM inference windows.

## Key Architectural & Strategic Findings

### 1. The Proliferation of Coding Agent Observability & Skills (Cats 04, 34, 44)
The 2026 FOSS ecosystem is dominated by an explosion of agentic developer tooling. Categories 04 (Agent Skills), 34 (Coding Agent Observability), and 44 (Self-Learning Agent Skills) collectively account for over 800 repositories. Projects like `observal`, `optim-plans`, `numbat`, `truedeck`, and `codejury` illustrate the transition from monolithic chat interfaces to modular, skill-based, multi-agent supervisory architectures.

### 2. Modern Web & Desktop Spine: Svelte 5 and Tauri 2 (Cats 50, 51)
Categories 50 (Svelte Frontend UI/UX) and 51 (Desktop Development with Tauri 2) exhibit strong traction, counting 100 and 125 tools respectively. Tauri v2 has emerged as the clear standard for native cross-platform AI workbenches (e.g. `OpenSlides`, `devtools-x`, `pake`), leveraging Rust backends with Svelte 5 runes for high-performance, low-memory footprints compared to traditional Electron apps.

### 3. Real-Time Backends: Postgres, Supabase, and Fastify (Cats 09, 10)
Over 450 projects populate the Postgres and Supabase ecosystems. Modern setups heavily favor TypeScript + Node.js/Fastify for high-throughput APIs (`fastify`, `bun-sqlgen`, `better-drizzle`) coupled with Supabase Realtime and pgvector for low-latency live synchronization and semantic retrieval.

**Product Description Text**:
> A categorized collection of awesome Unity open source on GitHub (800+)

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> A categorized collection of 800+ open-source Unity repositories hosted on GitHub, organized to help developers quickly discover tools, effects, and utilities for game development. The repository addresses the difficulty of finding quality, community-vetted Unity assets by curating and classifying them into major categories including Shaders, Editor Extensions, UI components, Scripts, Mobile-specific tools, and miscellaneous utilities like ECS, physics, AI, and multiplayer systems. Each category is further broken down into granular subcategories—such as water shaders, post-effects, tilemap editors, joysticks, and object pooling—making it easy to locate resources for specific needs. Subcategories cover specialized topics like force fields, hologram shaders, color pickers, asset bundles, async/await patterns, and reverse engineering tools, providing both learning material and production-ready code. Ideal for Unity developers of all skill levels—from beginners seeking reference implementations to experienced developers looking for advanced techniques in shader programming, editor tooling, and performance optimization. The collection showcases projects from notable contributors like keijiro alongside community submissions, spanning classic CG/ShaderLab code and modern ShaderGraph workflows, with clear categorization enabling efficient browsing without requiring exhaustive searching across GitHub.

> SCSKiller is a free, open-source Windows application that eliminates shader compilation stutter in PC games by pre-compiling shaders into the GPU driver's cache before gameplay. When a game encounters a new visual effect, the driver must compile the corresponding shader, causing the frame to pause; SCSKiller extracts shaders from game files, determines the required graphics pipelines, and compiles them in a separate process while the game is closed. The tool supports DirectX 12 titles on both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, as well as DirectX 11 games on NVIDIA, and automatically detects installed games from major storefronts including Steam, Epic, GOG, Ubisoft Connect, EA, Xbox, and Battle.net. Key features include automatic detection of stutter-prone games, automatic re-compilation after driver updates, an optional in-game recorder for titles whose shader files aren't accessible, per-session frame time analysis, and an opt-in community shader database for Patreon supporters. The app is available as a standard installer or portable archive, requires no administrator privileges, and is intended for anyone who wants smoother, stutter-free PC gaming performance without modifying game files or interacting with anti-cheat systems.

> Blender MCP is an open-source plugin that bridges Blender 3D with any Large Language Model through the Model Context Protocol, enabling prompt-assisted 3D modeling, scene creation, and manipulation. It provides two-way socket-based communication between an LLM client (such as Claude Desktop, Cursor, or VS Code) and Blender via two components: a Blender addon that runs a socket server inside Blender, and a Python MCP server implementing the protocol. Installation requires Blender 3.0+, Python 3.10+, and the `uv` package manager, with the addon enabled through Blender's preferences. The tool targets 3D artists, developers, and AI enthusiasts seeking to automate or assist Blender workflows through natural language, and is distributed under the MIT license.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Champ is an ECCV 2024 framework for animating static human images using 3D parametric guidance from SMPL models, enabling controllable motion transfer without requiring video or motion clips of the target subject. The system leverages multiple guidance signals—including depth maps, normal maps, DWPose skeletal keypoints, and semantic maps—rendered from 3D human meshes to drive a diffusion-based image animation model fine-tuned from Stable Diffusion V1.5. It supports both inference with pre-trained weights and full model training, producing temporally coherent animations suitable for applications in virtual avatars, content creation, and digital human synthesis. The repository includes a ComfyUI wrapper, Blender add-ons for SMPL processing, a Replicate demo, and pre-rendered motion samples for quick testing. Researchers and developers working on controllable image generation, 3D-aware animation, or human avatar synthesis will find it particularly useful, though it requires substantial GPU resources (tested on A100 and RTX 3090 with 20GB VRAM recommended for longer sequences). The codebase is built on PyTorch and Diffusers, with installation supported via either pip or Poetry on Ubuntu 20.04/Windows 11 systems.

> OpticalModeler is an evidence-gated Agent Skill that converts 2D photonics schematics into physically auditable 3D optical tables inside Blender. It treats optical topology, real apertures, manufacturer CAD, fasteners, load paths, fiber routing, and artifact lineage as strict acceptance gates rather than decorative details, producing fail-closed evidence through reopened-scene audits, ray/BVH checks, hashes, manifests, and explicit PASS/BLOCKED/UNVERIFIED states. Key features include post-first hardware assembly from verified table holes, optical-center and splitter-plane solving, branch-continuity verification, proof-of-instance validation before propagation, and consistent packaging of renders, GLB files, reports, and compliance matrices. The target users are photonics researchers, optical engineers, and laboratory staff who need trustworthy, reproducible reconstructions of complex optical setups for documentation, review, or planning purposes. The technology stack centers on Blender for 3D rendering and physics simulation, STEP/CAD asset integration, ray tracing with BVH acceleration, and an Agent Skills framework (installable via `npx skills add`) that guides autonomous agents through a six-stage reconstruction and audit pipeline. Released under the MIT License, it serves as an independent community tool with a sanitized G1/G2 case study demonstrating end-to-end workflow from schematic input to verified 3D output.

Key features include a deliberate render order (cheap-before-expensive composition, picture-locked audio), resume-safe run manifests, a Mission Control click-to-approve gallery, a derived content brief you sign off on a storyboard, a copy linter, per-brand motion personalities, export matrices in 16:9/9:16/1:1/4:5, and paste-ready post kits with SRT/VTT sidecars. Built on Remotion for video composition, Playwright for app capture, headless Blender for 3D logo reveals, ElevenLabs for voiceover and music, and ComfyUI for optional AI backdrops—each feeder degrades cleanly when its dependency is missing. Brands are pure data (`brands/<id>.json` with zod-validated tokens), so onboarding a new product is a JSON file plus a logo mark component rather than a fork. Targets indie developers, small product teams, and founders launching products who want consistent, on-brand launch assets from a single terminal command.

It packages a streamlined workflow into a local Node.js review app and seven agent Skills, distributed as a runnable ZIP, where users review images and 3D candidates at checkpoints while a Codex-based AI agent (GPT-6.1 Sol or GPT-6 Astra) handles Tripo operations, Blender work, and rigging in between. Workflow stages include image painting in four views, selecting head and body candidates, proportion adjustments, and walk-cycle motion verification, all managed through a single `project.charakit` file with no manual exports. The stack runs on Node.js 22+ with a Chromium browser, integrates Tripo for 3D generation, and uses Blender 5.2 with the VRM Add-on and Blender MCP for weight transfer, physics, and final export. Indie creators, VTuber enthusiasts, and developers needing custom 3D avatars would benefit from this tool, though it requires a Tripo account and Codex CLI with image generation capabilities.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Mixamo-llm-mocap converts any locked-camera video—live footage or AI-generated—into forward-kinematics animation retargeted onto any Mixamo character, including two-performer fight plates split into separate tracks. The pipeline chains pose estimation via GVHMR (SMPL-X mesh recovery) into a 10-stage scriptable workflow covering landmark extraction, beat detection from numeric output, a JSON action spec for support foot, fist timing and rest blends, direction-preserving retargeting onto a user-measured rig profile, FK aim with foot planting through Blender MCP, automated QA for pops, skate and root drift, frame-by-frame comparator against the source video, two-character collision checking against skinned meshes in Blender, and final side-by-side preview rendering. A new motion is a small JSON spec rather than code, and worked examples include a kung-fu form, jump combos, a 360° spin kick and a two-fighter duel. The tool targets indie animators, mocap-adjacent creators and AI-agent pipelines that need honest Mixamo-compatible output without mocap suits, manual keyframing or IK hacks, with every stage exposed as a CLI or socket call and a pitfalls document encoding prior failure patterns.

#### 1. [superpowers](https://github.com/obra/superpowers) (`obra/superpowers`)
- **Official URL**: [https://github.com/obra/superpowers](https://github.com/obra/superpowers)
- **Primary Language**: `Shell` | **Stars**: `★ 264,520` | **License**: `MIT`
- **Catalog Provenance**: Channel: *ManuAGI - AutoGPT Tutorials* | Video: *Top Open-Source GitHub Projects : Ghidra, Home Assistant, LibreChat, Coder & supervision #293* | Published: *2026-09-19*
- **Attached Keywords**: `ai, agent, testing, framework, code-review`
- **GitHub Topics**: `ai, brainstorming, coding, obra, sdlc, skills, subagent-driven-development, superpowers`

**Product Description Text**:
> Superpowers, productivity toolkit for developers. Superpowers is an open-source collection of utilities and workflow enhancements designed to improve developer productivity

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Superpowers is an agentic skills framework and software development methodology that transforms coding agents into disciplined engineering collaborators rather than eager code generators. It solves the problem of AI coding assistants jumping straight into implementation by enforcing a structured workflow: brainstorming requirements into validated designs, isolating work in git worktrees, breaking plans into bite-sized tasks, and executing via subagent-driven development with strict test-driven development (RED-GREEN-REFACTOR). Skills trigger automatically, so the agent naturally applies TDD, YAGNI, and DRY principles while often running autonomously for hours without deviating from approved plans. The framework installs as a plugin across numerous AI coding harnesses, including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Devin CLI, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, OpenCode, and Hermes Agent. It targets software developers and engineering teams who want consistent, high-quality output from AI coding tools without micromanaging every step, and is offered by Primate Radiant with commercial support available for enterprise users.


#### 2. [andrej-karpathy-skills](https://github.com/multica-ai/andrej-karpathy-skills/blob/main/CLAUDE.md) (`multica-ai/andrej-karpathy-skills`)
- **Official URL**: [https://github.com/multica-ai/andrej-karpathy-skills/blob/main/CLAUDE.md](https://github.com/multica-ai/andrej-karpathy-skills/blob/main/CLAUDE.md)
- **Primary Language**: `Not specified` | **Stars**: `★ 198,543` | **License**: `Unspecified / FOSS`
- **Catalog Provenance**: Channel: *Cooly* | Video: *Cooly's Chrome Links* | Published: *2026-09-02*
- **Attached Keywords**: `ai, claude-code, documentation, plugin, markdown, llm, cursor`

**Product Description Text**:
> Claude code workflows inspired by Karpathy principles. Andrej Karpathy skills is an open-source collection of Claude code skills and development guidelines inspired by software engineering practices associated with Andrej Karpathy

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> A single-file solution for improving Claude Code behavior, derived from Andrej Karpathy's observations on common LLM coding pitfalls such as making unchecked assumptions, overcomplicating code, and making orthogonal edits. The repository distills these issues into four principles encoded in a `CLAUDE.md` file: Think Before Coding (surface assumptions and tradeoffs), Simplicity First (avoid speculative features and bloated abstractions), Surgical Changes (touch only what the task requires), and Goal-Driven Execution (transform imperative tasks into verifiable success criteria with test-driven loops). Developers using Claude Code, Cursor, or similar AI coding assistants install it either as a reusable Claude Code plugin via the marketplace or by downloading the markdown file directly into any project. The implementation is purely a markdown configuration document, with no runtime dependencies, making it trivial to merge with project-specific instructions. The guidelines explicitly trade speed for caution, encouraging judgment on trivial tasks while reducing costly mistakes on substantive work.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Context Mode is an MCP server that tackles the context window bloat problem faced by AI coding agents, where raw tool outputs (Playwright snapshots, GitHub issues, log files) can consume 40% or more of the available context within minutes. It achieves a 98% reduction in token usage by sandboxing tool outputs, keeping raw data out of the model context while preserving access to computed results. Session continuity is maintained through an SQLite-backed event store indexed with FTS5 and queried via BM25, so agents retain awareness of file edits, tasks, and user decisions across compaction cycles without re-dumping history into context. The "Think in Code" paradigm replaces dozens of file-read tool calls with a single sandboxed script that outputs only the relevant result, and routing enforcement is applied automatically across 17 supported platforms via MCP plus hook integrations. It is licensed under ELv2, distributed as an npm package and Claude Code plugin, and targets engineering teams using AI coding assistants in environments such as Claude Code, Cursor, and other MCP-compatible clients.

> Specification and documentation for Agent Skills

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Agent Skills is an open standard, originally developed by Anthropic, for packaging specialized knowledge and workflows into portable folders that AI agents can load on demand. Each skill is centered on a `SKILL.md` file containing metadata and procedural instructions, with optional bundled scripts, references, and assets. Agents interact with skills through progressive disclosure: at startup they only load skill names and descriptions for discovery, read full instructions only when a task matches, and execute bundled code as needed—minimizing context usage while supporting many skills simultaneously. The format addresses the gap between increasingly capable agents and the domain-specific, company-, or user-specific context they require to perform real work reliably and consistently. Skills enable reusable domain expertise, repeatable multi-step workflows, and cross-product compatibility across any skills-compatible agent. The repository contains the format specification and documentation, licensed under Apache 2.0 for code and CC-BY-4.0 for documentation, with contributions welcome from the broader ecosystem.

It targets a core failure mode in agentic LLMs: instruction files that describe values without prescribing procedure. Instead of telling a model to "be careful and verify," the method enforces concrete steps with thresholds: classify the ask, name a verification criterion before acting, gather primary-source evidence in parallel, commit to one recommendation, make the smallest correct change, verify by observation, and report the outcome first with honest caveats. Results show the method's value concentrates at traps (spec-vs-test conflicts, false "work complete" reports, unauthorized deploys, weak-tier executors) with the lift being inversely proportional to model capability, meaning it helps smaller models most. At its core is a hypothesis-tree framework where a Coordinator agent maintains a persistent Idea Tree of results, failure modes, and distilled insights, while Executor agents implement and test individual hypotheses in isolated git worktrees, ensuring the main branch is never touched until gains are confirmed. A structured six-step "arbor cycle" (observe, ideate, select, dispatch, backpropagate, decide) enables the system to learn from its own runs, recall prior findings, and check novelty against literature via keyless APIs like alphaXiv before spending compute. Across benchmarks like BrowseComp, Terminal-Bench 2.0, and MLE-Bench Lite, Arbor reportedly outperforms Claude Code and Codex by roughly 2.5× on the same compute budget. The agent is highly flexible, supporting providers such as Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek, Gemini, Qwen, and Ollama through LiteLLM, and is accessible as a Python CLI, an MCP integration for Claude Code/Codex, or a standalone Agent Skill Suite—making it usable both by ML researchers seeking automated experiment optimization and by engineers wanting a steerable, dashboard-monitored autonomous coding assistant.

Its standout capability is per-item visibility tracking via IntersectionObserver, letting applications react to which items are currently on screen (e.g., disabling arrows at the edges or highlighting the active tab).

The component is framework-agnostic about styling: items are plain user components with their own CSS and required `itemId` props, while the library only supplies a separate CSS import for the scroll container itself. Navigation works through scrollbar, touch, mouse wheel, drag, or programmatic APIs (`scrollToItem`, `scrollPrev`, `scrollNext`, `apiRef`), with a `VisibilityContext` and hooks (`useIsVisible`) for component-level access to state.

Built on native scrolling rather than a carousel engine, it intentionally omits snap physics, spring animations, or built-in autoplay/infinite-loop props — those are documented as ~60-line recipes on top of the public API. The library is SSR-safe (with official Next.js/RSC guidance), TypeScript-native, RTL-aware, and supported by task-scoped AI agent skills and a Storybook with live-editable examples. **Product Description Text**:
> ProductSpec is an open standard for defining product intent in software projects, providing a portable "Product Harness" that defines what to build, what not to build, how to prove completion, and when intent changes. It bridges product, engineering, and AI coding agents (like Claude, Codex, and Cursor) by structuring intent into machine-readable fields (scope, acceptance criteria, AI evals, success metrics) while keeping human-reasoning sections readable. The ecosystem includes companion artifacts: Agent Run receipts for recording what happened during agent execution and Decision Traces for capturing consequential changes over time. **Product Description Text**:
> Zero-config web reader for AI agents: clean Markdown from WeChat, GitHub, X and regular sites, optional headless-browser fallback, robots.txt aware; CLI + MCP server via one uvx line. Created Oct 5. GH: 1★, pushed 2026-10-05.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Agent-web-fetch is a Python toolkit that fetches web pages for AI agents using a tiered "cheapest-first, escalate-only-when-needed" strategy, preferring official site APIs, then simple HTTP requests with realistic browser headers, then identity switching (desktop Chrome, mobile Safari, WeChat browser), and only finally a headless browser. It distinguishes itself from typical scrapers by inspecting every response to detect block types—Cloudflare challenges, CAPTCHAs, login walls, paywalls, rate limits, soft 404s, and JS-only pages—and returning machine-readable `blocked_reason` codes instead of letting agents hallucinate summaries of verification pages. Extraction combines multiple strategies (trafilatura, Mozilla Readability, JSON-LD, embedded JS state like `__NEXT_DATA__`, Open Graph metadata, and site-specific adapters) and picks the richest result, with candidates logged for debugging. It ships as a CLI (`awf`), an MCP server (`awf-mcp`) for Claude Code and Cursor, an installable Agent Skill file, and a Python library, making it useful for developers building AI agents that need reliable, honest web reading without burning tokens on blocked or empty pages. Optional Playwright integration handles true JavaScript-rendered content but refuses to solve CAPTCHAs or bypass authentication, and a strict robots.txt mode supports batch crawling scenarios.

> AgentConnect is a developer-focused connectivity layer for AI agents that aims to make it trivial to expose, discover, and chain MCP-compatible tools and resources across services. It provides a unified address surface where agents can find the right endpoint for a given capability without hard-coding bespoke integrations, and it standardizes authentication, schema discovery, and session handling so an agent can compose remote capabilities as if they were local. The project targets developers building multi-agent or tool-using systems who need a single place to publish capabilities and let any compliant agent consume them, with first-class support for common protocol patterns and minimal configuration to get started.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> AgentConnect is an open-source, Apache-2.0-licensed platform that lets teams deploy multiple AI agents — such as Claude Code, Codex, DeepSeek, or any ACP-compatible runtime — directly into their existing chat channels (Slack, Discord, Telegram, GitHub, Linear, etc.) where work already happens. It solves the fragmentation problem of running isolated AI assistants by providing a unified control plane for managing a "fleet" of agents, with built-in support for agent roles, scheduled jobs (daemons/cron), PR review workflows, and inter-agent collaboration where agents can call on one another. Key capabilities include a console for monitoring agents, sessions, schedules, and daemons; scoped permissions and per-agent tool/skill access; native, managed, or bring-your-own memory (Mem0); connectors to 1,000+ apps via MCP; and skills like code review and web search. Developers and engineering, DevOps, support, and payments teams use it to triage issues, run community support, customize code review, keep watch via cron and webhooks, and build AI-native apps from clients like claude.ai over MCP. The stack centers on an ACP (Agent Connect Protocol) standard for agent interoperability, with an MCP-compatible connector surface, OpenTelemetry observability, Logto for SSO, and deployment options ranging from self-hosted daemons to managed Cloud execution or private enterprise installs.

> agenthatch is a command-line tool that compiles SKILL.md files — the markdown format used by AI agent platforms like Claude Code and Codex CLI — into standalone, runnable Python agents. It addresses core shortcomings of raw SKILL.md, including context-window pollution between skills, lack of validation, high token costs from loading full skill bodies into every prompt, and degraded behavior as the number of skills grows. The tool runs a three-phase pipeline: deterministic parsing of the markdown, parallel inference through six specialized LLM harnesses that produce a validated AHSSPEC (Agent Hatch Standard Specification), and Jinja2-based code generation that emits a pip-installable Python package with typed tools, MCP integration, and a CLI entry point. A post-generation self-review pass smoke-tests each tool with mock parameters and regenerates broken function bodies, while a runtime PlanLayer layer handles execution. The intended users are developers building multi-skill agent systems who want deterministic, debuggable, and scalable agents rather than prompt-engineered prose interpreted by an LLM at every turn.

> Anti-slop is an opinionated Oxlint plugin for TypeScript and JavaScript teams that want unsafe shortcuts to fail in CI. Its rules reject chained assertions, unknown widening, module mocking, and assertions without a nearby safety explanation

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Anti-slop is an opinionated Oxlint ruleset that rejects low-evidence, low-signal patterns in TypeScript and JavaScript, such as chained type assertions, unsafe dictionary types, runtime `typeof` narrowing, and module mocking. It is meant to be vendored into a repository rather than installed as an npm dependency, giving teams full ownership to read, modify, and maintain the rules to fit local conventions. An accompanying agent skill automates the copy, version-matching with any existing Oxlint installation, configuration merge, and validation. Optional Effect-specific rules enforce architectural policies like discouraging direct service constructor imports in favor of contextual Layer yields, activated only in projects that depend on Effect. The rules are intentionally local, leveraging Oxlint's ESTree and lexical-scope APIs without a TypeScript type checker, making them fast and suitable for any TypeScript or JavaScript codebase seeking stricter, more explicit coding standards.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> apk-reverse is an Agent Skill (for Claude Code, Codex, and compatible harnesses) that performs Android APK reverse engineering, debloating, ad removal, dex-level patching, and runtime/server protocol analysis. It targets the recurring failure mode where AI models read instructions, agree with them, and then revert to first-principles reasoning, replacing open-ended advice with a procedural framework of four override rules (R1–R4), four verification gates (G1–G4), a symptom-index-driven stop-signal catalog, and a two-strike rule to prevent repeated identical mistakes. The skill distinguishes client-side feasibility from server-enforced paywalls, selects the safest patch layer for a given change, and catches silent failures such as repacked APKs whose signed requests are rejected because the signing key is derived from the original certificate. It is packaged for progressive disclosure, with a short decision-oriented `SKILL.md`, on-demand reference files (e.g. `advanced-unpacking.md`), parameterized Python scripts such as `doctor.py` for environment diagnosis, and Markdown coverage, with a Python Markdown Markdown Android toolchain spanning MT Manager, LSPosed, Frida (including Stalker and RPC service-ification), and OLLVM-flattened native analysis, aimed at security researchers, reverse engineers, and developers debugging or hardening Android applications.

Security and governance are first-class concerns: API keys are kept in the operating system keychain rather than config files or the cloud, every tool is fingerprinted to flag definition changes ("rug pulls") and tool-poisoning attacks, and per-tool toggles plus a unified permission policy let users hide destructive tools fleet-wide. The app is distributed as a native desktop client for Windows, macOS, and Linux (MIT licensed) and adds cross-client management of agent rules and permission presets, with live observability for latency, errors, and audit logs. **Product Description Text**:
> Unlazy is an agent skill that makes done mean the checks actually passed. Before substantial work, it turns requirements into an acceptance ledger with runnable commands and expected output

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> unlazy is a completion-discipline skill for AI coding agents that addresses the gap between "AI said it was done" and "the work is actually verified." It enforces a gate-based workflow where the agent must write an acceptance ledger (GATES.md) up front, declaring runnable checks with explicit shell commands, expected outputs, and evidence before declaring a task complete.

The core mechanism is a Node.js checker (`gate-check.mjs`) that parses a Markdown ledger, executes each `CHECK:` command, and only marks a gate as passed when the process exits 0 and the `EXPECT:` pattern matches the combined output. Successful output is fingerprinted (SHA-256/byte-count) but not echoed or persisted, and each gate binds tightly to its exact command, working directory, shell, PATH, and platform via approval records stored in `~/.unlazy/approved`.

Key features include a non-executing `--status` mode for inspection, an advisory `gate-lint.mjs` to catch weak ledger patterns, a scoped orchestration format (`.unlazy/<scope>/`) for parallel multi-agent pipelines with declared file ownership and path leases, and a rolling-dispatch model that unblocks newly eligible work as verified leaves complete.

It is aimed at developers using agents like Claude Code or Codex CLI on substantial refactors, migrations, or multi-package work, and it ships with no third-party runtime dependencies, requiring only Node 16+.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> ZooWork is an AI agent delivery platform from Serendipity One that enables domain experts and forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) to package their knowledge, methods, and tools into autonomous agents that execute real business work. Its Agent Builder lets users define roles, company knowledge, working SOPs, delivery standards, and tool permissions via a chat-driven interface, producing reusable "Agent Skills" such as Brand Planner, Store Ops, CRM, and Research Associate agents. These agents run on a managed, cloud-native runtime that integrates with frontier models (OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM), connects to enterprise systems (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, Jira, GitHub, ERPs, etc.) via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and operates inside isolated sandboxes with human approval gates, least-privilege access, and full audit trails. The platform also exposes a Managed Agent API for embedding agents into existing apps and a ZooData service that turns any URL into structured, agent-ready JSON for e-commerce, finance, and social intelligence. It targets retail chains, marketing agencies, cross-border e-commerce, smart manufacturing, and investment research teams — offering 7-day pilot deployment and industry playbooks that have reportedly cut tasks like stockout detection and proposal drafting from hours or days to under an hour.

**Product Description Text**:
> Your own personal AI assistant. Any OS. Any Platform. The lobster way. 🦞

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> OpenClaw is a personal AI assistant that runs on your own devices and connects through the messaging platforms you already use. It centralizes AI models, tools, skills, plugins, channels, and companion apps through a local Gateway, functioning as either an individual assistant or a shared team deployment. The Gateway serves as the control plane for sessions, events, tool execution, and messaging connections, with access available through a web Control UI, CLI, and terminal UI. OpenClaw supports WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord, Google Chat, Signal, iMessage, and other channels, while companion nodes can provide voice, camera, screen, canvas, and device-local capabilities. It is designed for users who want a private, extensible assistant, as well as trusted teams operating a shared gateway, and supports both hosted and local model providers. The stack is TypeScript/Node.js, distributed as an npm package with installer support for macOS, Linux, Windows, and WSL2; development uses a pnpm workspace.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Hermes Agent is a self-improving AI agent built by Nous Research that addresses the limitation of stateless AI assistants by implementing a continuous learning loop — it autonomously creates skills from experience, refines them during use, and builds a deepening user model across sessions through [Honcho](https://github.com/plastic-labs/honcho) dialectic modeling and FTS5 session search with LLM summarization. The agent is model-agnostic, supporting providers like Nous Portal, OpenRouter, OpenAI, and custom endpoints, with seamless switching via `hermes model` and no vendor lock-in. It features a full terminal UI with multiline editing and slash commands, a unified messaging gateway spanning Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, and voice memo transcription, and a built-in cron scheduler for unattended automations delivered to any channel. Hermes runs on seven backends — local, Docker, SSH, Singularity, Modal, Daytona, and Vercel Sandbox — with serverless hibernation that costs nearly nothing when idle, making it deployable on everything from a $5 VPS to GPU infrastructure, plus native Windows support. It also serves research workflows through batch trajectory generation and compression for training tool-calling models. Ideal users are developers, researchers, and power users who want a persistent, platform-flexible assistant rather than a single-machine chatbot. The technology stack centers on Python 3.14 with Node.js, ripgrep, and FFmpeg, distributed under the MIT lic

Version 2.0 is a complete rewrite that evolved from a deep-research framework into a general-purpose agent platform capable of researching, coding, and creating. Core features include extensible skills and tools (with Claude Code integration), session goals, manual context compaction, sub-agent delegation, sandbox file system access, context engineering, and long-term memory persistence. It can be deployed via Docker or local development, connects to IM channels through MCP servers, and includes a terminal workbench (TUI), scheduled tasks, and an embedded Python client. DeerFlow is aimed at developers, researchers, and power users who need to automate complex multi-step workflows that exceed the scope of single LLM calls, offering deployment diagnostics, support bundles for issue reporting, and configuration through an interactive setup wizard.

**Product Description Text**:
> AI agents running research on single-GPU nanochat training automatically

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> autoresearch enables fully autonomous AI-driven experimentation on a simplified single-GPU implementation of nanochat, a small-scale LLM training pipeline. Instead of a human manually tweaking code, an AI agent autonomously modifies train.py—the single file containing the GPT model, Muon+AdamW optimizer, and training loop—runs a fixed 5-minute training budget, evaluates the result via validation bits-per-byte (val_bpb), and keeps or discards the change in a continuous experimental loop. The core methodology shifts the researcher's role from editing Python to curating program.md, a Markdown "skill" that instructs the agent on experimental strategy, allowing approximately 12 experiments per hour or ~100 experiments overnight. It is designed for ML researchers and engineers experimenting with agentic AI workflows who want to explore autonomous research loops on a self-contained PyTorch stack requiring only a single NVIDIA GPU and Python 3.10+. The minimal codebase consists of just prepare.py (fixed data prep and utilities) and train.py (the agent's editable surface), deliberately constrained for comparability across hardware and reviewable diffs.

**Product Description Text**:
> clawk provides coding agents like Claude Code and Codex with their own disposable Linux virtual machine instead of running them directly on the host machine, eliminating the tradeoff between babysitting permission prompts and running with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`. By booting a lightweight VM (via Apple's Virtualization.framework on macOS or Firecracker on Linux) with only the user's code directory mounted in, the agent gets root access inside the sandbox while the host filesystem, keychain, and sensitive files remain completely inaccessible. An allow-listed outbound network and forwarded ssh-agent let agents push to GitHub without keys ever entering the guest, while arbitrary package installs, system modifications, and even nested container workloads are safe because destruction is cheap and recreable from the host's persisted conversation state. Designed for developers who want autonomous agents to run real builds, tests, and dev servers without compromising host security, clawk requires no Docker daemon, Dockerfile, or devcontainer configuration—just `cd` into a repo and run `clawk`. Written in Go 1.26+, it supports multi-repo workflows via git worktrees, automatic VM suspension for idle sandboxes, and can even run Docker or Kubernetes tooling inside the guest when hardware virtualization is available.

**Product Description Text**:
> Loop.js is a framework for "loop engineering," addressing the core problem that simply running an agent in a `while (true)` loop doesn't guarantee convergence. Users define a goal and its verification criteria, and the engine iteratively executes "Rounds" of work using fresh context and disk-based memory until a separate, read-only "Verify" agent—a skeptical judge—confirms the goal is met, ensuring the worker never grades its own homework. Key features include declared budget guards (rounds, USD, timeouts) with strict defaults to prevent runaway costs, idempotent disk-based state with a Lock mechanism for overlap-safe restarts, and a CLI scheduler (`loop cron`) that integrates with local system cron or deploys to Modal's cloud without requiring a daemon. The framework is designed for developers and teams who need to autonomously build, maintain, or audit tasks—such as shipping software, generating daily reports, executing trading strategies, or enforcing chores—where deterministic verification is required. It is built as a Node.js/TypeScript package (`@loop.js/core`), runs agents via the Claude Agent SDK, and uses Modal for optional cloud execution and persistent storage.

The architecture begins with a scoping phase that clarifies user intent and produces an initial draft, followed by a denoising loop where a supervisor agent identifies weaknesses, delegates parallel research tasks to worker agents, and integrates new findings to progressively improve the report. Self-correction is enforced through a Red Team agent that attacks draft logic for flaws and an Evaluator agent that scores quality, creating a convergence check that drives iteration until a high-quality standard is met. A context pruning mechanism manages state entropy, preventing the system from being overwhelmed as research accumulates. Built in Python with LangChain, LangGraph, and Pydantic, the framework provides a reusable blueprint for researchers, developers, and AI practitioners seeking to build multi-agent systems that produce well-sourced, thoroughly vetted research outputs.

> LoopFlow transforms Claude Code from an interactive assistant into an autonomous system by letting users define recursive goals in YAML, where pipelines of agents iterate until a verification gate passes, a budget is exhausted, or an attempt limit is hit. It addresses three core problems of unattended agentic loops: self-grading (solved by independent gate agents with distinct personas that must output `VERDICT: PASS`), runaway cost (solved by hard USD budgets enforced both by the runner and Claude Code's `--max-budget-usd` flag), and cross-run amnesia (solved by per-loop Markdown memory files appended after every run and injected into subsequent prompts). Additional features include opt-in git worktree isolation to prevent working-tree collisions and session-id logging so any step can be resumed via `claude --resume` for full auditability. The tool is aimed at developers and engineering teams who want reliable, cost-controlled automation for tasks like test-and-fix cycles, debt auditing, and documentation synchronization, and runs locally with Node.js 18+ plus an authenticated Claude Code installation—no API keys, daemons, or cloud dependencies required.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Benzi is an AI coding harness that replaces context-window dumping with a compiler-backed code index built on tree-sitter, parsing every file to produce a precise, queryable map of symbols, call edges, references, and class inheritance before any question is answered. It supports ten programming languages plus HTML, CSS, and DOM-JS, is language- and model-agnostic, compiles locally, follows a bring-your-own-key (BYOK) model, and is compatible with the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The agent interacts with code through ~35+ structured tools such as `profile`, `get_callers`, `backflow`, `trace_path`, and `skim_source`, enabling O(1) symbol resolution instead of grepping, embedding, or signature mapping. Every edit is gated against the real parser, with broken parses triggering automatic reverts, and changes are verified by a runtime tracer running alongside flag-tested blast-radius tests. On the SWE-bench Verified benchmark, Benzi achieved 391/500 (78.2%) resolved instances for a total cost of $37.33 using DeepSeek v4-flash, with a median of just 379 source lines read per task and 97% of input tokens served from cache. Developers and AI coding tool builders seeking efficient, structurally aware code intelligence across large codebases are the primary audience, demonstrated by live demos including a greenfield Python/JS dating app, an index of 923k lines of the real VS Code TypeScript source, and a public web demo accepting any GitHub repo.

It is built in Python, distributed via `pip install doberman-core`, and is aimed at developers, security teams, and organizations deploying autonomous or semi-autonomous coding agents who need enforceable, auditable authorization rather than post-hoc advisory guardrails.

> mini-AGI is a byte-level language model designed for continual learning on consumer hardware, running end-to-end on a single GPU with as little as 8 GB of VRAM. It tackles two persistent barriers to owning a personal model: the impossibility of training from scratch on a single card, and catastrophic forgetting when fine-tuning on new data. Key techniques include paging weights from disk to GPU on demand (so capacity is bounded by free disk rather than VRAM), Mixture-of-Experts style growth and pruning that expands architecture during training when capacity is saturated, and a shared read/serve code path for inference. Users point it at a corpus via a dashboard and it trains as it reads, with every checkpoint and sample logged for inspection. The stack is Python with a custom training loop using Adam, evals tracked in nats/bits-per-character, and per-domain held-out losses (arithmetic, code, chat, chess, reasoning, stories, Wikipedia) for monitoring. It's aimed at hobbyists, independent researchers, and anyone who wants to train or continually extend a model on their own machine, currently at toy scale with weights unpublished until a full corpus pass completes.

It is built around three guarantees that most chat-with-search interfaces do not offer: an enforced cost or token budget (every model and search call is reserved in a database ledger before it runs and settled after, so `--usd 0.50` is a hard ceiling rather than an estimate), quote-verified claims (a claim whose quote cannot be located verbatim in its source is rejected at extraction, and claims that turn out unsupported on later reading are flagged rather than silently dropped), and a local-data privacy boundary (CSV/TSV/JSON/JSONL files can be analysed without their contents ever leaving the machine, with only aggregates covering at least five rows allowed back, logged via `mole crossings`). Projects dispatch a `/cloud` workflow with a branch and prompt; a self-hosted Actions runner brings up the project's `docker-compose.yml`, runs the Claude session in an isolated container built from the repository's image (`ghcr.io/qrafttech/agent`), and lets Claude push commits and open pull requests itself—including stacked PRs via `gh stack`, with any unpushed work salvaged as a draft. Each session resumes from the branch's prior state, runs in parallel across branches, starts the app's servers and validates them in headless Chromium (chrome-devtools MCP), and can be watched, steered, or stopped from the Claude app over Remote Control. Security is enforced by design: the container holds a single fine-grained token scoped to one repository, with no sudo, no published ports, and no Docker socket. **Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> SafeExec MCP is a security gateway that sits between AI agents (Claude, GPT, or any MCP-compatible client) and production tools, evaluating every tool call against a declarative policy before execution. It solves the risk of agents wielding unrestricted access to sensitive systems like Active Directory, financial platforms, or deployment pipelines, requiring no modifications to existing tools or clients. Calls are routed through one of four policy tiers: `block` rejects dangerous actions immediately, `ask` pauses for human approval via a webhook, `notify` executes while alerting auditors, and `allow` runs without notification, all governed by a "deny by default" philosophy. Key features include HMAC-signed approval tokens to prevent replay attacks, append-only JSONL audit logging, tool wrapping with zero shell-expansion risk (`shell=False`), a condition expression language for fine-grained rules, and a standalone web UI for human reviewers. The system is built in Python 3.11+ using a YAML-based configuration model (`tools.yaml`, `policy.yaml`, `secrets.env`, `server.yaml`), SQLite for approval state, and supports both stdio and streamable-HTTP transports. DevOps teams, security engineers, and anyone deploying autonomous agents against production infrastructure would benefit most from adopting it.

> ToolReplay is a Python CLI tool that audits recorded transcripts of AI agent tool calls to detect non-determinism, redundant invocations, and permission overreach. It parses JSONL session logs and reports the earliest divergence point where a deterministic re-run would disagree with the record, flags identical repeated calls that produced no new information, and identifies any tool usage exceeding a declared permission scope. The tool operates through distinct subcommands—`replay` for self-contained reproducibility checks, `scope` for permission auditing against a separate declaration file, `seal` and `verify` for hash-chained transcript integrity, and `version`. Built as a zero-dependency Python 3.11+ package with no network access, it is suited for AI safety engineers, agent developers, and red-teamers who need to verify that autonomous agents behaved reproducibly and within their authorized tool boundaries. A sample session in the repository demonstrates all three finding types in a single six-call transcript, illustrating the tool's diagnostic output format.
