> ZeroSearch is a reinforcement learning framework developed by Alibaba's Tongyi Lab that trains large language models to effectively use search engines without requiring real-time API calls during training, eliminating costly search API expenses. The approach converts an LLM into a retrieval module through supervised fine-tuning, enabling it to generate both relevant and noisy documents in response to queries and simulate search engine behavior. A curriculum rollout mechanism progressively increases retrieval difficulty to strengthen the model's reasoning capabilities over time. Experiments demonstrate that ZeroSearch outperforms models trained with real search engines across in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks while generalizing well across base and instruction-tuned LLMs of various sizes. The framework supports multiple reinforcement learning algorithms, including REINFORCE, GRPO, and PPO, and is compatible with both Wikipedia and Google search simulation. It solves the typical pain point of retrieval stacks that require a separate vector service, duplicated data, and additional backup, replication, and authorization boundaries by keeping retrieval alongside the source data. It is built by Evokoa, distributed under Apache-2.0, and targeted at teams that want production-grade semantic and hybrid search without bolting on a second system.

> KADATH is an open-source framework that applies Darwinian evolution to AI agent development, automatically generating and progressively improving agents optimized for a user-specified goal. Rather than relying on a single prompt or agent design, it spawns a population of agents that compete across multiple generations, are independently graded against a measurable benchmark, learn from top performers, mutate, and reproduce—producing increasingly capable solutions through repeated selection. The architecture is split into two strictly separated layers: a non-evolving kernel that controls scheduling, benchmarking, grading, lineage, isolation, and resource management, and the organisms (evolvable agents) whose full framework—including system prompt, Python code, tools, and dependencies—forms the genome subject to mutation between epochs. Agents can inspect but not modify their own code during a run, preventing them from manipulating their fitness scores. Key features include a model-driven Architect that converts natural-language goals into validated, contract-conforming benchmarks with locked hashes; an interactive CLI for configuring goals, epoch duration, population size, and iteration counts; full Git-based genome lineage with duplicate-rejection; read-only container isolation per organism; rich telemetry combining high-level activity logs with detailed execution traces; and automatic first-boot provisioning of PostgreSQL, MinIO, LiteLLM, and SearXNG services via Docker.

> LatticeDB is an embedded, single-file property-graph database that unifies graph traversal, HNSW vector similarity search, and BM25 full-text search in a single query language, eliminating the need to stitch together separate systems for connected, semantic, and textual data. It targets local-first applications with relationship-heavy workloads—Graph RAG, agent memory, and personal knowledge tools—and offers zero-config operation with a WAL-backed, single-writer embedded model. Additional capabilities include image and video search, file uploads (PDFs, text, images), domain-specific searches, smart suggestions, contextual widgets (weather, stocks, calculations), and locally stored search history. The application is distributed as a Docker image bundled with SearxNG for quick deployment, with a slim variant available for users running their own SearxNG instance, and can also be built from source using Node.js. Vane is aimed at privacy-conscious developers, researchers, and everyday users who want a self-hosted alternative to commercial AI search tools without sacrificing features like multi-provider model support and rich result presentation.

> `wacrawl` creates read-only snapshots of the macOS WhatsApp Desktop databases, importing chats, contacts, messages, and media metadata into a local SQLite archive for fast searching, structured exports, private browsing, and encrypted Git backups without connecting to WhatsApp's network. It supports full-text search across message text, chat and sender names, and media titles, with filters for date ranges, media attachments, and JSON output for automation. A built-in web viewer binds exclusively to `127.0.0.1`, requires a per-run access key, and serves as a read-only interface to the archive. Encrypted backups use deterministic JSONL shards compressed and encrypted to X25519 age recipients before pushing to a Git remote, with content-deduplicated media blobs and verified restores. The tool targets developers, archivists, and privacy-conscious users who need portable local access to their WhatsApp history on macOS 13+ (with cross-platform support for archives and backups). Written in Go 1.27+ using `modernc.org/sqlite` for pure-Go database access, it is distributed via Homebrew, `go install`, and pre-built binaries for macOS, Linux, and Windows.

> Wake is a native desktop application that unifies scattered coding-agent session histories from tools like Claude Code, Codex CLI, Qoder, Cursor, OpenCode, and others into a single browsable, searchable interface. It solves the problem of agents stashing transcripts across dozens of hidden directories (`~/.claude`, `~/.codex`, `~/.gemini`, etc.), reading them all in a strictly read-only fashion without ever modifying the original files. Built with Rust and the GPUI framework, it offers full-text search via SQLite FTS5 trigram indexing, transcript rendering with tree-sitter code highlighting, one-click resume back into the original terminal at the correct project directory, and insights like GitHub-style activity heatmaps and model leaderboards. Privacy is central: session data stays local, credential files are never touched, and no background network requests occur. The app is primarily macOS-focused with experimental Linux and Windows support, targeting developers who juggle multiple AI coding assistants and want a single window into their complete agent conversation history.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> wigolo is a local-first web intelligence layer for AI agents that provides search, fetch, crawl, extract, caching, similarity lookup, and autonomous research loops without requiring API keys or sending data to the cloud. It runs entirely on the user's machine—storing all data in `~/.wigolo/` and bundling its own browser engine and on-device ML models—so there is no metered billing tied to agent usage. The tool integrates with coding assistants and agent frameworks such as Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, VS Code, Windsurf, and Zed via MCP, and also exposes a REST endpoint and SDK for self-hosted agents, LangChain, CrewAI, LlamaIndex, and the Vercel AI SDK. Core search and fetch capabilities use 18 direct search engine adapters with rank fusion and ML reranking, while a tiered fetch router escalates from plain HTTP to a headless browser when it encounters anti-bot challenges or JavaScript-heavy pages. Results return with byte-exact provenance, citation IDs, and an explainable evidence score, and weak results are flagged automatically. Setup is handled through a single `npx wigolo init` command, with optional LLM provider keys (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, or local Ollama) only needed for the `research` and `agent` synthesis tools.

Developed by Microsoft and published on PyPI, MarkItDown requires Python 3.10+ and benefits from a virtual environment to manage its optional dependencies.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Crossfoot reads invoice PDFs by separating the problem of locating data from the problem of transcribing it: a language model points at where values sit on the page, ordinary code copies the values from the PDF text, and the document's printed totals are used to prove the read. A successful read produces a small JSON "reading spec" describing the layout, so subsequent invoices of the same shape are processed in milliseconds with no model call and no network access. Accountants, finance teams, AP automation developers, and anyone who needs to convert varied PDF invoices into trustworthy structured data benefit most, since the tool detects tampering or OCR mistakes via built-in cross-foot checks and returns unproven reads with the failed check rather than silently producing wrong totals. Built on Node.js 20+ as an ES module package, it exposes a CLI (`crossfoot invoice.pdf`) and a programmatic API (`createReader`), with pluggable model adapters (Anthropic supported) and pluggable spec stores. Output preserves the document's original text formatting for numbers and dates, names columns after the headings printed on the page, and returns a typed result with `proven`, `rows`, `via`, and `problem` fields so callers can decide how to handle unproven documents.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Long-document search with Jev and PageIndex locates the page that answers a question in lengthy reports (300+ pages) without vector databases or embeddings. It works by combining Jev's `Choice` primitive—multiple-choice question answering with per-option probabilities—with PageIndex's hierarchical tree representation of documents. Jev navigates the tree level by level, making one small `Choice` over a handful of children at each step until reaching the relevant page, bypassing the 32k-token and 255-option limits that break flat page search on long documents. The repository provides both a simple flat page search for short PDFs and a full tree-search implementation with deeper hierarchies, top-K candidate selection, and answer verification. Researchers, analysts, and developers who need to query financial reports, legal documents, or other lengthy PDFs can run it directly via the included `page_search.py` script. The technology stack centers on the TypeSafe SDK (Jev model) and the PageIndexClient API, with PyPDF for PDF extraction.

It addresses a fundamental flaw in most document datasets—where structure is reverse-engineered from rendered text via OCR and heuristics—by generating images, SVGs, and PDFs with fully known layout from the start. > typesafe-computer-use is an open-source CLI tool that drives a macOS machine toward a goal expressed in plain English, costing roughly $0.0002 per decision by replacing screenshot-based frontier-model reasoning with a hybrid deterministic/classifier architecture. It captures the screen, runs Vision OCR on it, parses macOS accessibility tree data for actionable controls, merges the two sources into a numbered list, and asks the TypeSafe decision API for an action choice from a constrained set — only invoking a writer model (Claude) when free text genuinely needs generation, such as emails or URL proposals. The repository targets developers, researchers, and automation engineers building cheap desktop agents, benchmarks included that show 130x–390x cost reduction and 3.7x–40x speedup over raw Claude Opus 4 on computer-use tasks. Stopping heuristics include a confidence threshold, no-op detection, a maximum step count, and a mouse-failsafe in the screen corner; setup requires macOS 14+, Python 3.12+, and the `uv` package manager. The stack is Python with Vision OCR for text extraction, AppleScript/AX for app state, and Anthropic Claude as the writer model, with TypeSafe providing the core decision-making primitive.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> ha.mr is a client-side URL compressor that shortens links and generates compact QR codes directly in the browser, requiring no backend or database. It minimizes link length by stripping common components like protocols and "www." prefixes, encoding ports as raw numeric values, and applying Huffman coding to frequently used second-level domains, top-level domains, and URL segments. For QR codes specifically, it leverages the alphanumeric character set to produce smaller, more efficient codes than typical generators. The tool runs entirely in JavaScript, making it suitable for privacy-conscious users, developers needing lightweight link sharing, or anyone wanting offline-capable URL shortening. The project deliberately maintains a minimal scope, relying on plain JavaScript rather than heavy frameworks, and emphasizes transparency in contributions.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Hink is a link shortening service designed for hackers, utilizing Git commit hashes as unique identifiers for short links. The system stores the original long URL within the commit message of an empty Git commit. When a short link is accessed, the service retrieves the long URL by fetching the corresponding `.patch` file from GitHub and performing a redirect. It is implemented as a serverless script worker, compatible with platforms like Cloudflare Workers and Tencent EdgeOne. Hink integrates with Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) to provide access statistics and analytics for traffic monitoring. Advanced usage allows for API interaction to dynamically update the long URL associated with a specific commit hash.

**Product Description Text**:
> Firecrawl is an open-source API designed to power AI agents by providing reliable methods for searching, scraping, and interacting with the web at scale. It specializes in extracting clean, structured data from complex web pages, including handling JavaScript-heavy content and managing proxy issues automatically. The service offers features such as web search, comprehensive scraping, and advanced interaction capabilities like clicking and scrolling. Firecrawl ensures LLM-ready output, delivering data in formats like markdown, JSON, and screenshots, which significantly reduces token usage for AI applications. Built for speed and reliability, it acts as a crucial data layer, enabling AI agents to gather and process real-time web information efficiently.

**Product Description Text**:
> Puppeteer, browser automation library for Chrome and Firefox. Puppeteer is an open-source browser automation library that provides a high-level API for controlling browsers programmatically

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Puppeteer is a powerful JavaScript library designed to control Chrome and Firefox browsers programmatically. It provides a high-level API that leverages the DevTools Protocol to automate browser tasks. By default, Puppeteer operates in headless mode, allowing for efficient automation in server environments. The library enables developers to perform complex interactions, such as navigation, element manipulation, and data extraction. It is widely used for web scraping, testing, and end-to-end automation workflows. Installation options include installing the full package or the lighter `puppeteer-core` library.


#### 3. [playwright](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright) (`microsoft/playwright`)
- **Official URL**: [https://github.com/microsoft/playwright](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright)
- **Project Homepage**: [https://playwright.dev](https://playwright.dev)
- **Primary Language**: `TypeScript` | **Stars**: `★ 93,777` | **License**: `Apache-2.0`
- **Catalog Provenance**: Channel: *ManuAGI - AutoGPT Tutorials* | Video: *Top Dev Tool Projects : Playwright, CapRover, Santa, Octane, Webiny & Project AIRI* | Published: *2026-08-06*
- **Attached Keywords**: `automation, testing, playwright, typescript, browser`
- **GitHub Topics**: `automation, chrome, chromium, e2e-testing, electron, end-to-end-testing, firefox, javascript, playwright, test, test-automation, testing, testing-tools, web`

**Product Description Text**:
> Playwright is a framework for web testing and automation that enables developers to drive Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit with a single, unified API. It eliminates the need for browser-specific code, supporting use cases ranging from end-to-end testing and browser automation scripts to AI-driven agent workflows. Key features include auto-waiting actions, web-first assertions, resilient locators, parallel test execution across multiple browsers, isolated browser contexts per test, and a Trace Viewer for debugging with screenshots, videos, and DOM snapshots. The ecosystem extends beyond the core test runner to include Playwright CLI for coding agents and Playwright MCP, a Model Context Protocol server that lets AI assistants control browsers through structured accessibility snapshots. Developers, QA engineers, and AI agent builders use Playwright for cross-browser testing, web scraping, PDF generation, and screenshot capture. Built on Node.js with TypeScript support, it distributes via npm and integrates with editors through a VS Code extension.


#### 4. [sherlock](https://github.com/sherlock-project/sherlock) (`sherlock-project/sherlock`)

**Product Description Text**:
> Hunt down social media accounts by username across social networks

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Sherlock is an open-source OSINT (Open Source Intelligence) command-line utility for locating usernames across more than 400 social networks and websites. It solves the problem of fragmented online presence by allowing users, security researchers, and investigators to input a single username and quickly determine where that handle is registered, eliminating the need to manually check each platform individually. Key features include support for searching multiple usernames simultaneously, flexible output formats (text, CSV, XLSX, JSON), wildcard character substitution with `{?}` for similar username variations, proxy support for anonymous queries, and the ability to open results directly in a browser. The tool can be installed via pip, pipx, uv, Docker, or through community-maintained packages for distributions like Debian, Ubuntu, Kali, and BlackArch. Written primarily in Python, Sherlock is widely used by penetration testers, journalists, digital forensics professionals, and privacy-conscious individuals conducting username reconnaissance or brand protection investigations.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Crawl4AI is an open-source Python web crawler and scraper that converts web pages into clean, LLM-ready Markdown optimized for RAG pipelines, AI agents, and data extraction workflows. It addresses the gap between basic scrapers and costly proprietary services by offering fast, controllable crawling with features like smart Markdown generation, BM25 filtering, citation handling, deep crawling with crash recovery, and structured extraction using any LLM. The tool provides an async browser pool, session management, proxies, hooks, and adaptive crawling that learns site patterns to explore only relevant content, making it suitable for developers building AI applications that need reliable web data ingestion. Deployment is flexible with a CLI, Docker support, and zero API key requirements, while an upcoming Cloud API promises large-scale extraction at lower cost. Built on Python with Playwright for browser automation, Crawl4AI is targeted at AI engineers, data scientists, and researchers needing production-grade web scraping without vendor lock-in.

**Product Description Text**:
> Give your AI agent eyes to see the entire internet. Read & search Twitter, Reddit, YouTube, GitHub, Bilibili, XiaoHongShu — one CLI, zero API fees.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Agent Reach is a CLI capability layer that gives AI agents one-command access to read and search across the open web—including Twitter/X, Reddit, YouTube, Bilibili, GitHub, XiaohongShu, RSS feeds, and arbitrary webpages—without paid API keys. It solves the fragmentation problem of platform-specific anti-scraping defenses, login requirements, and unstable upstream CLIs by acting as a thin router that selects, installs, and health-checks the most reliable free backend for each site, with automatic fallbacks when one tool breaks (e.g., swapping yt-dlp for bili-cli when Bilibili's anti-bot blocked yt-dlp in mid-2026). It automatically generates realistic HTTP headers (User-Agent, Accept, Sec-Fetch-*, etc.) across various browsers, operating systems, devices, and locales via the bundled `header-generator` package, while also handling ALPN protocol negotiation to use HTTP/2 like modern browsers. > Fortress is a stealth Chromium fork designed to prevent scrapers and browser-based AI agents from being blocked by bot-detection systems. It tackles the core fingerprinting problem by patching ~34 surfaces directly in Chromium's C++ source (Blink, V8, BoringSSL, ANGLE/D3D11) rather than overlaying JavaScript shims, so every spoofed getter returns `[native code]` consistently across main frames, iframes, and Web Workers—defeating detection methods like the `Runtime.enable` leak and realm-mismatch probes. The engine ships as a drop-in CDP binary on port 9222, allowing existing Playwright, Puppeteer, or any CDP client to connect without code changes; tunable `--uxr-*` flags expose per-persona controls for GPU, screen, timezone, hardware, and Client-Hints, with full Windows-persona coherence (keyboard layout, media devices, JA3/JA4 TLS shape) enforced at launch. It passes CreepJS (0% headless/stealth), Sannysoft, BrowserScan, and live Cloudflare Turnstile challenges, and is distributed via pip, npm, Docker, and an MCP server exposing 29 stealth-browser tools for AI agents. The target users are web-scraping engineers, automation developers, and teams building browser-using LLM agents who need their infrastructure to present as ordinary Chrome to protected sites. Released under BSD-3 with reproducible, gauntlet-gated builds, Fortress rebases monthly against upstream Chromium to stay current.

> DLBrowser is a self-healing, metered web access layer for AI agents, exposed as a single MCP that delivers 11 tools (`fetch`, `scrape`, `crawl`, `search`, `screenshot`, `smart_extract`, etc.) to hosts like Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Cline, and Codex via one `npx dlbrowser connect` command. It tackles the core failure mode of agentic browsing—where Cloudflare challenges, captchas, and JavaScript-heavy pages silently return empty strings—through a five-backend escalation cascade (`curl_cffi` → `tls_client` → `playwright` → `nodriver`/CDP → `firecrawl`) that starts with a ~50ms HTTP request and only climbs the ladder when a block is detected, reportedly passing 3/5 Cloudflare-protected test sites without ever launching a browser. Every run is atomically metered through reservation-based credits (1 credit per page regardless of backend, flat pricing where competitors charge 5–7× for JS rendering), with backend, latency, and estimated cost logged to a queryable OpenTelemetry-compatible ledger so teams can answer "what does our web data cost?" The router learns per-domain success/latency/cost over time, returns clean markdown instead of raw HTML (~77% fewer tokens measured on a Wikipedia page), and supports LLM-driven structured extraction against local models without cloud keys. Distributed as a PyPI/npm package under MIT, it offers a hosted gateway at `api.dekryptlabs.com` alongside full self-host parity for teams that need their data to stay in-house.

A single `scrape.py` script requires only the standard library and Python 3.9+, accepting filters by district id, cuisine id, or free-text keywords, with configurable request delays and support for batched runs when fetching the full city of roughly 28,800 open restaurants. Each row contains the venue's English and Chinese names and addresses, GPS coordinates, HKD price bands, weekly opening hours, cuisines, dish types, phone numbers, bookmark counts, review totals, smile/cry counts, and overall scores, with documented completeness rates for every field. The scraper correctly handles several quirks of the live site, including ignored `page` parameters, the 10,000-result paging ceiling, duplicate listings for relocated venues, a score of `0` meaning "not scored," and anti-bot challenges, persisting already-collected rows if a run must abort. Researchers, journalists, data analysts, and developers building local-recommendation or mapping products for the Hong Kong F&B market are the likely users, and a hosted version on Apify is offered for those who prefer a no-code, scheduled, REST-accessible alternative.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Patchright is a patched, drop-in replacement for Microsoft's Playwright testing and automation framework, specifically engineered to evade bot detection systems during browser automation. It addresses common detection vectors that expose standard Playwright as an automated tool, including the Runtime.enable leak (avoided by executing JavaScript in isolated execution contexts), Console.enable leaks (disabled entirely), and command-line flag leaks (such as removing `--enable-automation` and adding `--disable-blink-features=AutomationControlled`). The tool additionally patches general codebase leaks and uniquely supports interaction with elements inside closed shadow roots, a capability absent from vanilla Playwright. Patchright only supports Chromium-based browsers, with Firefox and WebKit remaining unsupported. It is distributed as the core driver repository alongside companion client libraries for Python, Node.js, and a community-maintained .NET package, targeting developers engaged in web scraping, automated testing, and large-scale browser automation tasks requiring stealth.

It requires Python 3.10+ and is targeted at developers building scrapers, automated testers, and researchers who need stealthy, flexible browser control without the overhead of traditional WebDriver frameworks.

#### 1. [open-webui](https://github.com/open-webui/open-webui) (`open-webui/open-webui`)
- **Official URL**: [https://github.com/open-webui/open-webui](https://github.com/open-webui/open-webui)

- **Catalog Provenance**: Channel: *Cooly* | Video: *Cooly's Chrome Links* | Published: *2026-09-02*
- **Attached Keywords**: `ai, mcp, ollama, self-hosted, rag, llm`

**Product Description Text**:
> User-friendly WebUI for LLMs (Formerly Ollama WebUI)

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Open WebUI is a self-hosted, offline-capable AI platform that provides a user-friendly interface for interacting with large language models, addressing the need for a private, extensible alternative to cloud-based AI chat services. It supports multiple LLM runners including Ollama and any OpenAI-compatible API (such as LMStudio, GroqCloud, and vLLM), enabling users to mix local and remote inference providers seamlessly. Key features include built-in Retrieval Augmented Generation with support for nine vector databases, granular role-based access control, a robust plugin system with MCP integration, and collaborative tools like shared Channels, persistent memory, and AI-assisted scheduling. It offers a responsive Progressive Web App with full Markdown/LaTeX rendering, voice and video calling capabilities, image generation, multi-model conversations, and enterprise-ready features such as LDAP/SSO/SCIM authentication, OpenTelemetry observability, and horizontal scalability via Redis. Ideal for developers, IT administrators, research teams, and enterprises seeking a customizable, secure AI deployment, Open WebUI is built with a modern technology stack including Python (backend), Svelte/TypeScript (frontend), Docker/Kubernetes support, and flexible database options (SQLite or PostgreSQL).


#### 2. [huginn](https://github.com/huginn/huginn) (`huginn/huginn`)
- **Official URL**: [https://github.com/huginn/huginn](https://github.com/huginn/huginn)
- **Primary Language**: `Ruby` | **Stars**: `★ 49,809` | **License**: `MIT`
- **Catalog Provenance**: Channel: *Cooly* | Video: *Cooly's Chrome Links* | Published: *2026-09-02*
- **Attached Keywords**: `monitoring, api, automation, web, self-hosted, alternatives`
- **GitHub Topics**: `agent, automation, feed, feedgenerator, huginn, monitoring, notifications, rss, scraper, twitter, twitter-streaming, webscraping`

**Product Description Text**:
> Create agents that monitor and act on your behalf. Your agents are standing by!

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Huginn is a self-hosted, open-source platform for building automated agents to monitor web activity and perform tasks on your behalf. Often described as a hackable, privacy-focused alternative to IFTTT and Zapier, it lets users create agents that read feeds, scrape pages, and trigger actions via a directed graph of events. It integrates with numerous services, including Twitter, Slack, RSS, email, Twilio, JIRA, MQTT, and Amazon Mechanical Turk, while supporting custom JavaScript agents and webhook-based workflows. Use cases range from weather alerts and deal tracking to sentiment spike notifications and complex multi-step human-in-the-loop tasks. The platform is built in Ruby on Rails, uses MySQL or PostgreSQL, supports Docker-based deployment, and is extensible through standalone Ruby gems, appealing to developers, sysadmins, and privacy-conscious users who want full control over their automation stack.

**Product Description Text**:
> The communications platform that puts data protection first.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Rocket.Chat is a secure, open-source communications platform designed for mission-critical team collaboration and controlled information exchange. It solves the need for private, compliant communication across colleagues, external organizations, and customers through real-time messaging, voice, asynchronous collaboration, and federation. Key features include end-to-end encryption, identity and access management, role- and attribute-based controls, self-hosting, cloud and air-gapped deployments, plus extensive customization through Apps-Engine and external integrations. It serves governments, defense, critical infrastructure, regulated enterprises, and other organizations with strict data-protection requirements. The TypeScript platform supports web, desktop, and mobile experiences and can be deployed with Docker, Podman, Kubernetes, or managed cloud hosting.


#### 4. [novu](https://github.com/novuhq/novu) (`novuhq/novu`)
- **Official URL**: [https://github.com/novuhq/novu](https://github.com/novuhq/novu)

- **GitHub Topics**: `agents, communication, email, inbox, infrastructure, nodejs, notification-center, notifications, novu, push-notifications, react, reactjs, sms, transactional`

**Product Description Text**:
> Open-Source Notification Platform. Embeddable Notification Center, E-mail, Push and Slack Integrations.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Novu is an open-source communication infrastructure platform that unifies messaging across multiple channels—including Inbox/In-App, Email, SMS, Push, Chat, Slack, Microsoft Teams, Telegram, and WhatsApp—through a single API and conversation model. It solves the problem of fragmented, one-way notifications by enabling bidirectional, thread-based conversations suitable for both traditional product notifications and AI agent interactions. Key features include an embeddable real-time `<Inbox />` component, a workflow engine with branching and conditions, a digest engine for batching notifications, a no-code email editor, and embeddable user preference controls. Its Agent Communication Infrastructure (ACI) allows developers to connect any custom or framework-based agent (Claude, AI SDK, LangGraph, etc.) to end-user channels without building per-platform webhook handlers. Novu is built for developers and product teams who need scalable, multi-channel messaging, supporting 20+ email providers and offering SDKs for React with additional framework support in development.

**Product Description Text**:
> BitChat is a decentralized, peer-to-peer messaging app that operates without accounts, phone numbers, or central servers, instead using a dual-transport architecture: a local Bluetooth Low Energy mesh network for offline communication and the Nostr protocol for global, internet-based messaging. It solves the problem of censorship-resistant and infrastructure-independent communication, making it suitable for protests, disaster response, remote areas, and privacy-conscious users who need to chat without relying on traditional cellular or internet service providers. The app supports location-based channels defined by geohash coordinates (city, neighborhood, block, etc.) and offers IRC-style commands like `/msg` and `/who` for a familiar chat interface. Private messages are secured with Noise Protocol end-to-end encryption over Bluetooth and a custom XChaCha20-Poly1305 envelope for Nostr fallback, with automatic routing that prefers Bluetooth when available and falls back to internet relays when not. Additional features include LZ4 message compression, adaptive battery modes, an emergency triple-tap wipe, and full native support for iOS and macOS via Swift and Xcode.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> The Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol is an open standard that enables communication and interoperability between autonomous AI agents built on diverse frameworks and operated by different organizations. It addresses the challenge of agent silos by providing a common language for agents to discover each other's capabilities, negotiate interaction modalities, and collaborate on long-running tasks without exposing internal state, memory, or proprietary tools. Built on JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP(S), A2A supports agent discovery via standardized "Agent Cards," flexible interaction patterns including synchronous, streaming (SSE), and asynchronous push notifications, and rich data exchange with text, files, and structured JSON. The protocol is designed for enterprise readiness with built-in security, authentication, and observability, and complements the Model Context Protocol (MCP) by enabling agent-to-agent collaboration rather than agent-to-tool interaction. Official SDKs are available in Python, Go, JavaScript, Java, .NET, and Rust, with supporting samples and a partnership-backed DeepLearning.AI course. A2A is intended for AI developers, framework creators, and enterprises building multi-agent systems who need standardized, vendor-neutral interoperability across heterogeneous agentic applications.

Unlike the official MCP Inspector, which connects as its own client, mcpsnoop sits directly in the data path, so it sees exactly what the real client and server exchange, including hung calls, malformed JSON-RPC frames, and silent tool failures. It works by wrapping stdio servers with a shim that forwards bytes verbatim while copying frames to a hub and TUI, and it can also run as a reverse proxy for streamable-HTTP servers, where it surfaces HTTP status codes, auth challenges, and routing errors as visible frames. Key features include filtering and searching by status (e.g., `status:401`), secret redaction via config file, multi-format session export (JSON, HTML, HAR, OTLP), CI-friendly checks, session diffing and replay, tool-definition baseline comparison for detecting drift, and shell completions for bash, zsh, fish, and PowerShell. The tool is built in Go as a single static binary with no runtime dependencies, installable via `go install`, Homebrew, or prebuilt releases, and ships with a built-in demo mode for immediate exploration. **Product Description Text**:

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Sherlock is an open-source OSINT (Open Source Intelligence) command-line utility for locating usernames across more than 400 social networks and websites. It solves the problem of fragmented online presence by allowing users, security researchers, and investigators to input a single username and quickly determine where that handle is registered, eliminating the need to manually check each platform individually. Key features include support for searching multiple usernames simultaneously, flexible output formats (text, CSV, XLSX, JSON), wildcard character substitution with `{?}` for similar username variations, proxy support for anonymous queries, and the ability to open results directly in a browser. The tool can be installed via pip, pipx, uv, Docker, or through community-maintained packages for distributions like Debian, Ubuntu, Kali, and BlackArch. Written primarily in Python, Sherlock is widely used by penetration testers, journalists, digital forensics professionals, and privacy-conscious individuals conducting username reconnaissance or brand protection investigations.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> BettaFish (微舆) is a multi-agent public opinion analysis system designed to break information echo chambers, reconstruct the true landscape of online sentiment, and forecast future trends to support decision-making. It automatically monitors 30+ major domestic and international social media platforms (Weibo, Xiaohongshu, Douyin, Kuaishou, etc.) along with millions of public comments, using AI-driven crawlers that operate 24/7. The system employs four specialized agents—a Query Agent for web search, a Media Agent for multimodal content (including short videos), an Insight Agent for private database mining, and a Report Agent for generating polished HTML reports—that collaborate through a unique "forum" mechanism where a debate-host model mediates chain-of-thought exchanges between agents. Built from scratch in pure Python without relying on third-party agent frameworks, it features a modular, lightweight architecture that supports one-click deployment and easy customization for vertical domains such as finance and market analysis. The platform combines LLMs with fine-tuned models and statistical middleware for deeper analytical accuracy, and offers secure interfaces for integrating proprietary business data with public sentiment insights. Targeted at analysts, researchers, and decision-makers, BettaFish transforms complex, fragmented online discourse into structured intelligence through conversational queries.

**Product Description Text**:
> BitChat is a decentralized, peer-to-peer messaging app that operates without accounts, phone numbers, or central servers, instead using a dual-transport architecture: a local Bluetooth Low Energy mesh network for offline communication and the Nostr protocol for global, internet-based messaging. It solves the problem of censorship-resistant and infrastructure-independent communication, making it suitable for protests, disaster response, remote areas, and privacy-conscious users who need to chat without relying on traditional cellular or internet service providers. The app supports location-based channels defined by geohash coordinates (city, neighborhood, block, etc.) and offers IRC-style commands like `/msg` and `/who` for a familiar chat interface. Private messages are secured with Noise Protocol end-to-end encryption over Bluetooth and a custom XChaCha20-Poly1305 envelope for Nostr fallback, with automatic routing that prefers Bluetooth when available and falls back to internet relays when not. Additional features include LZ4 message compression, adaptive battery modes, an emergency triple-tap wipe, and full native support for iOS and macOS via Swift and Xcode.

**Product Description Text**:
> humanizer-stack is a two-pass pipeline for removing AI writing tells from outward-facing text, packaged as Claude Code Skills. It pairs a surface pass (vocabulary, punctuation, and phrasing fixes drawn from Wikipedia's Signs of AI writing plus a 3.2M-post Reddit analysis of copy tells) with a structural pass grounded in the StoryScope study, which detected AI-authored stories at 93.2% F1 using discourse-level features alone and found that span-level rewriting only reduced detection by 1.6 points. The structural pass runs six audits (theme explicitness, structural tidiness, emotion mode, reference specificity, reader engagement, and shape convergence) one at a time, since aspect-based checking recovered 95% of issues in the study's own pipeline against 68% for a combined pass. Two deterministic scanners (copy_scan.py and structural_scan.py) provide grep-able, hook-friendly checks with JSON output and strict-exit modes, while the skills themselves handle the judgment work. The target audience is writers, marketers, and developers using Claude Code who need outbound copy and short fiction that reads as though a person wrote it, aware that no tool makes text undetectable and that "show, don't tell" now functions as a machine signature. The stack is plain Python, markdown reference material, and shell installer, distributed under MIT with upstream CC BY-SA 4.0 obligations.

- **Attached Keywords**: `ai-agents, database, nextjs, postgresql, tools, nodejs, workflow, typescript`

**Product Description Text**:
> CRM flips the usual AI CRM design. The agent owns the work queue, while the interface shows what it found and why

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> An open-source CRM designed around AI agents rather than the other way around, solving the problem of CRMs that either ignore AI entirely or bolt a chatbot onto a static form. The agent runs as its own deployment on its own schedule, working through a queue (`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` leases), booking its own follow-ups, and persisting across redeploys. Its core principle is evidentiary discipline: tools report only what they observed, a ledger prices the evidence, strong signals write to the record, and weak ones become suggestions a human settles — no tool accepts a self-graded confidence score.

Key features include 18 authored tools, four versioned skill documents, a sandboxed shell with deny-all egress and no database credentials, and durable conversations on every contact, company, and deal that let users watch the agent work and answer its questions in place. Every outside data source is optional, with the system functioning on internal history alone; the Context API unlocks company brand data and LinkedIn identity resolution.

It's built for teams who want a CRM that actually keeps itself up to date without hallucinating customer facts, and for self-hosters who need to reconfigure without redeploying. The stack is a Turborepo monorepo on Bun: Next.js with shadcn/ui and nuqs on the front end, a NestJS tRPC API with mailbox sync, Prisma on Postgres, and Vercel's eve framework for the durable agent with Vercel Sandbox for execution.

The platform is designed for sales teams, customer support operations, and small-to-medium businesses seeking to automate WhatsApp-based workflows with intelligent, conversational AI. Key features include an interactive one-command installer for VPS deployment, built-in automation scheduling for rule-based triggers, optional two-factor authentication, an in-app update mechanism, and AI assistant guides for installation, customization, and prompt tuning. The technology stack centers on Next.js 16 with TypeScript for the application layer, Supabase for the database and authentication, and Docker-based containerization for self-hosted deployment, with integration support for OpenAI, Anthropic, and OpenRouter AI providers.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> wacrm is a self-hostable, open-source CRM template built specifically around the official WhatsApp Business API, letting small teams manage customer conversations, contacts, sales pipelines, broadcasts, and no-code automations from a single shared inbox. It is designed to be forked: users clone the repository, point it at their own Supabase project and Meta credentials, and deploy anywhere Node.js runs — with Hostinger's managed Node.js hosting recommended for one-click deployment. Core features include a multi-agent shared inbox with assignment and notes, Kanban-style deal pipelines, CSV contact imports with deduplication, Meta-approved broadcast templates with delivery tracking, a visual automation builder (triggers, branches, waits, webhooks), and an AI reply assistant powered by the user's own OpenAI or Anthropic key — optionally grounded in a knowledge base via Postgres full-text or pgvector retrieval. It also exposes a versioned REST API with scoped keys and an MCP server so external tools (Claude, Cursor) can interact with the CRM. The stack is deliberately conventional: Next.js 16 with the App Router, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind v4, Supabase for Postgres/Auth/Storage with row-level security on every table, and AES-256-GCM token encryption — aimed at developers and small businesses that want full ownership of their customer data without SaaS seat fees or vendor lock-in.

**Product Description Text**:
> A Git-compatible VCS that is both simple and powerful

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Jujutsu (jj) is a Git-compatible version control system designed to simplify version control workflows while offering powerful features for both new and experienced developers. It addresses common pain points of traditional VCS tools by treating the working copy as a commit—eliminating the need for staging areas and automating rebases and conflict resolution propagation through descendant commits. The system draws inspiration from Git, Mercurial, and Darcs, providing a fast, ergonomic command-line interface, a robust template language for output formatting, and first-class conflict tracking. A complete operation log enables undo functionality and easier debugging of repository history, while the design ensures safety under concurrent replication scenarios (e.g., syncing via Dropbox or rsync). Under the hood, jj uses Git repositories for physical storage, ensuring interoperability with existing Git-based tools and forges, while storing higher-level metadata like bookmarks in custom storage. Targeted at software developers working on projects ranging from small solo efforts to large team collaborations, jj is written in Rust and is developed by its own core team on GitHub.

> Worktrunk is a command-line tool that streamlines Git worktree management, enabling developers to run multiple AI coding agents (like Claude Code or Codex) in parallel without workspace conflicts. It addresses Git's notoriously clunky worktree UX by letting users address worktrees directly by branch name, with paths computed from a configurable template, eliminating repetitive commands. Core features include simplified worktree creation/switching/removal, an interactive picker with streaming CI status and diff previews, automated hooks for local workflows, LLM-generated commit messages, and efficient build cache sharing across worktrees via copy-on-write filesystems (APFS, btrfs, XFS). Additional quality-of-life tools support PR checkout, per-worktree dev server ports, branch-scoped variables, and one-command merge workflows that squash, rebase, merge, and clean up. Written in Rust, it installs via Homebrew, Cargo, Winget, Pacman, or Conda, and includes shell integration for seamless directory changes. Worktrunk targets developers managing 5-10+ parallel AI-driven tasks who need isolated, easily navigable working directories.

Their identity is checked and their billing process reviewed.' versions:   free-pro-team: '*' ---  ### About verified creators  A verified creator is an organization that {% data variables.product.company_short %} has checked. Anyone can share their apps with other users on {% data variables.product.prodname_marketplace %} but only organizations that are verified by {% data variables.product.company_short %} can sell apps. For more information about organizations, see "[About organizations](/github/setting-up-and-managing-organizations-and-teams/about-organizations)."  The verification process aims to protect users. For example, it verifies the seller's identity, checks that their {% data variables.product.product_name %} organization is set up securely, and that they can be contacted for support.   After passing the verification checks, any apps that the organization lists on {% data variables.product.prodname_marketplace %} are shown with a verified creator badge {% octicon "verified" aria-label="Verified creator badge" %}. The organization can now add paid plans to any of their apps. See "[Differences between GitHub Apps and OAuth Apps](/apps/differences-between-apps/)" for more details. - Apps should use the principle of least privilege and should only request the OAuth scopes and GitHub App permissions that the app needs to perform its intended functionality. For more information, see [Principle of least privilege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principle_of_least_privilege) in Wikipedia. - Apps should provide customers with a way to delete their account, without having to email or call a support person. - Apps should not share tokens between different implementations of the app. For example, a desktop app should have a separate token from a web-based app. Individual tokens allow each app to request the access needed for GitHub resources separately. - Design your app with different user roles, depending on the functionality needed by each type of user. For example, a standard user should not have access to admin functionality, and billing managers might not need push access to repository code. - Apps should not share service accounts such as email or database services to manage your SaaS service. - All services used in your app should have unique login and password credentials. - Admin privilege access to the production hosting infrastructure should only be given to engineers and employees with administrative duties. - Apps should not use personal access tokens to authenticate and should authenticate as an [OAuth App](/apps/about-apps/#about-oauth-apps) or a [GitHub App](/apps/about-apps/#about-github-apps):   - OAuth Apps should authenticate using an [OAuth token](/apps/building-oauth-apps/authorizing-oauth-apps/).   - GitHub Apps should authenticate using either a [JSON Web Token (JWT)](/apps/building-github-apps/authenticating-with-github-apps/#authenticating-as-a-github-app), [OAuth token](/apps/building-github-apps/identifying-and-authorizing-users-for-github-apps/), or [installation access token](/apps/building-github-apps/authenticating-with-github-apps/#authenticating-as-an-installation).  ### Data protection  - Apps should encrypt data transferred over the public internet using HTTPS, with a valid TLS certificate, or SSH for Git. - Apps should store client ID and client secret keys securely. We recommend storing them as [environmental variables](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environment_variable#Getting_and_setting_environment_variables). - Apps should delete all GitHub user data within 30 days of receiving a request from the user, or within 30 days of the end of the user's legal relationship with GitHub. - Apps should not require the user to provide their GitHub password. - Apps should encrypt tokens, client IDs, and client secrets.  ### Logging and monitoring  Apps should have logging and monitoring capabilities. App logs should be retained for at least 30 days and archived for at least one year. A security log should include:  - Authentication and authorization events - Service configuration changes - Object reads and writes - All user and group permission changes - Elevation of role to admin - Consistent timestamping for each event - Source users, IP addresses, and/or hostnames for all logged actions  ### Incident response workflow  To provide a secure experience for users, you should have a clear incident response plan in place before listing your app. We recommend having a security and operations incident response team in your company rather than using a third-party vendor. You should have the capability to notify {% data variables.product.product_name %} within 24 hours of a confirmed incident.  For an example of an incident response workflow, see the "Data Breach Response Policy" on the [SANS Institute website](https://www.sans.org/information-security-policy/). A short document with clear steps to take in the event of an incident is more valuable than a lengthy policy template.  ### Vulnerability management and patching workflow  You should conduct regular vulnerability scans of production infrastructure. You should triage the results of vulnerability scans and define a period of time in which you agree to remediate the vulnerability.  If you are not ready to set up a full vulnerability management program, it's useful to start by creating a patching process. For guidance in creating a patch management policy, see this TechRepublic article "[Establish a patch management policy](https://www.techrepublic.com/blog/it-security/establish-a-patch-management-policy-87756/)."  94  ...ent/developers/github-marketplace/security-review-process-for-submitted-apps.md  This file was deleted.    53  content/developers/github-marketplace/setting-pricing-plans-for-your-listing.md  @@ -1,6 +1,6 @@ --- title: Setting pricing plans for your listing intro: 'When [listing your app on {% data variables.product.prodname_marketplace %}](/marketplace/listing-on-github-marketplace/), you can choose to provide your app as a free service or sell your app. If you plan to sell your app, you can create different pricing plans for different feature tiers.' intro: 'When you list your app on {% data variables.product.prodname_marketplace %}, you can choose to provide your app as a free service or sell your app. If you plan to sell your app, you can create different pricing plans for different feature tiers.' redirect_from:   - /apps/adding-integrations/managing-pricing-and-payments-for-a-github-marketplace-listing/setting-a-github-marketplace-listing-s-pricing-plan/   - /apps/marketplace/managing-pricing-and-payments-for-a-github-marketplace-listing/setting-a-github-marketplace-listing-s-pricing-plan/ @@ -17,57 +17,52 @@ versions:   free-pro-team: '*' ---  ### About setting pricing plans  If you want to sell an app on {% data variables.product.prodname_marketplace %}, you need to request verification when you publish the listing for your app. During the verification process, an onboarding expert checks the organization's identity and security settings. Discussions empower a project's maintainers, contributors, and visitors to gather and accomplish the following goals in a central location, without third-party tools.  - Share announcements and information, gather feedback, plan, and make decisions - Ask questions, discuss and answer the questions, and mark the discussions as answered - Foster an inviting atmosphere for visitors and contributors to discuss goals, development, administration, and workflows  ![Discussions tab for a repository](/assets/images/help/discussions/hero.png)  You don't need to close a discussion like you close an issue or a pull request.  If a repository administrator or project maintainer enables discussions for a repository, anyone who visits the repository can create and participate in discussions for the repository. Repository administrators and project maintainers can manage discussions and discussion categories in a repository, and pin discussions to increase the visibility of the discussion. Moderators and collaborators can mark comments as answers, lock discussions, and convert issues to discussions. For more information, see "[Repository permission levels for an organization](/github/setting-up-and-managing-organizations-and-teams/repository-permission-levels-for-an-organization)."  For more information about management of discussions for your repository, see "[Managing discussions in your repository](/discussions/managing-discussions-for-your-community/managing-discussions-in-your-repository)."  ### About categories and formats for discussions  {% data reusables.discussions.you-can-categorize-discussions %} {% data reusables.discussions.about-categories-and-formats %} {% data reusables.discussions.repository-category-limit %}  For discussions with a question/answer format, an individual comment within the discussion can be marked as the discussion's answer. {% data reusables.discussions.github-recognizes-members %}  For more information, see "[Managing categories for discussions in your repository](/discussions/managing-discussions-for-your-community/managing-categories-for-discussions-in-your-repository)."  ### Best practices for discussions  As a community member or maintainer, start a discussion to ask a question or discuss information that affects the community. For more information, see "[Collaborating with maintainers using discussions](/discussions/collaborating-with-your-community-using-discussions/collaborating-with-maintainers-using-discussions)."  Participate in a discussion to ask and answer questions, provide feedback, and engage with the project's community. For more information, see "[Participating in a discussion](/discussions/collaborating-with-your-community-using-discussions/participating-in-a-discussion)."  You can spotlight discussions that contain important, useful, or exemplary conversations among members in the community. To join the conversation, see [`github/feedback`](https://github.com/github/feedback/discussions?discussions_q=category%3A%22Discussions+Feedback%22).  ### Further reading  - "[About writing and formatting on {% data variables.product.prodname_dotcom %}](/github/writing-on-github/about-writing-and-formatting-on-github)" - "[Searching discussions](/github/searching-for-information-on-github/searching-discussions)" - "[About notifications](/github/managing-subscriptions-and-notifications-on-github/about-notifications)" - "[Moderating comments and conversations](/github/building-a-strong-community/moderating-comments-and-conversations)" - "[Maintaining your safety on {% data variables.product.prodname_dotcom %}](/github/building-a-strong-community/maintaining-your-safety-on-github)"  50  ...community-using-discussions/collaborating-with-maintainers-using-discussions.md  @@ -0,0 +1,50 @@ --- title: Collaborating with maintainers using discussions shortTitle: Collaborating with maintainers intro: You can contribute to the goals, plans, health, and community for a project on {% data variables.product.product_name %} by communicating with the maintainers of the project in a discussion. permissions: People with read permissions to a repository can start and participate in discussions in the repository. versions:   free-pro-team: '*' ---  {% data reusables.discussions.beta %}  ### About collaboration with maintainers using discussions  {% data reusables.discussions.about-discussions %} If you use or contribute to a project, you can start a discussion to make suggestions and engage with maintainers and community members about your plans, questions, ideas, and feedback. For more information, see "[‎About discussions](/discussions/collaborating-with-your-community-using-discussions/about-discussions)."  {% data reusables.discussions.about-categories-and-formats %} Repository administrators and project maintainers can delete a discussion. You can also create a comment thread by replying to an individual comment that another community member made within the discussion, and react to comments with emoji. For more information about reactions, see "[About conversations on {% data variables.product.prodname_dotcom %}](/github/collaborating-with-issues-and-pull-requests/about-conversations-on-github#reacting-to-ideas-in-comments)."  You can block users and report disruptive content to maintain a safe and pleasant environment for yourself on {% data variables.product.product_name %}. For more information, see "[Maintaining your safety on {% data variables.product.prodname_dotcom %}](/github/building-a-strong-community/maintaining-your-safety-on-github)."  ### Prerequisites  Discussions must be enabled for the repository for you to participate in a discussion in the repository. For more information, see "[Enabling or disabling discussions for a repository](/github/administering-a-repository/enabling-or-disabling-github-discussions-for-a-repository)."  ### Creating a discussion  {% data reusables.discussions.starting-a-discussion %}  ### Marking a comment as an answer  Discussion authors and users with the triage role or greater for a repository can mark a comment as the answer to a discussion in the repository.  {% data reusables.discussions.marking-a-comment-as-an-answer %}  49  content/discussions/guides/best-practices-for-community-conversations-on-github.md  @@ -0,0 +1,49 @@ --- title: Best practices for community conversations on GitHub shortTitle: Best practices for community conversations intro: 'You can use discussions to brainstorm with your team, and eventually move the conversation to a discussion when you are ready to scope out the work.' versions:   free-pro-team: '*' ---  {% data reusables.discussions.beta %}  ### Community conversations in {% data variables.product.prodname_discussions %}  Since {% data variables.product.prodname_discussions %} is an open forum, there is an opportunity to bring non-code collaboration into a project's repository and gather diverse feedback and ideas more quickly. You can help drive a productive conversation by:  - Asking pointed questions and follow-up questions to garner specific feedback - Capture a diverse experience and distill it down to main points - Open an issue to take action based on the conversation, where applicable  For more information about opening an issue and cross-referencing a discussion, see "[Opening an issue from a comment](/github/managing-your-work-on-github/opening-an-issue-from-a-comment)."  ### Learning about conversations on GitHub  You can create and participate in discussions, issues, and pull requests, depending on the type of conversation you'd like to have.  You can use {% data variables.product.prodname_discussions %} to discuss big picture ideas, brainstorm, and spike out a project's specific details before committing it to an issue, which can then be scoped. Discussions are useful for teams if: - You are in the discovery phase of a project and are still learning which director your team wants to go in - You want to collect feedback from a wider community about a project - You want to keep bug fixes, feature requests, and general conversations separate  Issues are useful for discussing specific details of a project such as bug reports and planned improvements. For more information, see "[About issues](/articles/about-issues)." Pull requests allow you to comment directly on proposed changes. For more information, see "[About pull requests](/articles/about-pull-requests)" and "[Commenting on a pull request](/articles/commenting-on-a-pull-request)."  {% data reusables.organizations.team-discussions-purpose %} For more information, see "[About team discussions](/articles/about-team-discussions)."  ### Following contributing guidelines  Before you open a discussion, check to see if the repository has contributing guidelines. The CONTRIBUTING file includes information about how the repository maintainer would like you to contribute ideas to the project.  For more information, see "[Setting up your project for healthy contributions](/github/building-a-strong-community/setting-up-your-project-for-healthy-contributions)."  ### Next steps  To continue learning about {% data variables.product.prodname_discussions %} and quickly create a discussion for your community, see "[Quickstart for {% data variables.product.prodname_discussions %}](/discussions/quickstart)."  ### Further reading  - "[Setting up your project for healthy contributions](/articles/setting-up-your-project-for-healthy-contributions)" - "[Using templates to encourage useful issues and pull requests](/github/building-a-strong-community/using-templates-to-encourage-useful-issues-and-pull-requests)" - "[Moderating comments and conversations](/articles/moderating-comments-and-conversations)" - "[Writing on {% data variables.product.prodname_dotcom %}](/articles/writing-on-github)"  21  content/discussions/guides/finding-discussions-across-multiple-repositories.md  @@ -0,0 +1,21 @@ --- title: Finding discussions across multiple repositories intro: 'You can easily access every discussion you''ve created or participated in across multiple repositories.' versions:   free-pro-team: '*' ---  {% data reusables.discussions.beta %}  ### Finding discussions  1. Navigate to {% data variables.product.prodname_dotcom_the_website %}. 1. In the top-right corner of {% data variables.product.prodname_dotcom_the_website %}, click your profile photo, then click **Your enterprises**.   !["Your discussions" in drop-down menu for profile photo on {% data variables.product.product_name %}](/assets/images/help/discussions/your-discussions.png) 1. Toggle between **Created** and **Commented** to see the discussions you've created or participated in.  ### Further reading  - "[Searching discussions](/github/searching-for-information-on-github/searching-discussions)" - "[About discussions](/discussions/collaborating-with-your-community-using-discussions/about-discussions)" - "[Managing discussions for your community](/discussions/managing-discussions-for-your-community)"  32  content/discussions/guides/granting-higher-permissions-to-top-contributors.md  @@ -0,0 +1,32 @@ --- title: Granting higher permissions to top contributors intro: 'Repository administrators can promote any community member to a moderator and maintainer.' versions:   free-pro-team: '*' ---  {% data reusables.discussions.beta %}  ### Introduction  The most helpful contributors for the past 30 days are highlighted on the {% data variables.product.prodname_discussions %} dashboard, based on how many comments were marked as answers by other community members. Helpful contributors can help drive a healthy community and moderate and guide the community space in addition to maintainers.  ### Step 1: Audit your discussions top contributors  {% data reusables.repositories.navigate-to-repo %} {% data reusables.discussions.discussions-tab %} 1. Compare the list of contributors with their access permissions to see who qualifies to moderate the discussion.  ### Step 2: Review permission levels for discussions  People with triage permissions for a repository can help moderate a project's discussions by marking comments as answers, locking discussions that are not longer useful or are damaging to the community, and converting issues to discussions when an idea is still in the early stages of development. For more information, see "[Moderating discussions](/discussions/managing-discussions-for-your-community/moderating-discussions)."  For more information about repository permission levels and {% data variables.product.prodname_discussions %}, see "[Repository permissions levels for an organization](/github/setting-up-and-managing-organizations-and-teams/repository-permission-levels-for-an-organization)."  ### Step 3: Change permissions levels for top contributors  You can change a contributor's permission levels to give them more access to the tooling they need to moderate GitHub Discussions. accompanied by a detailed description stating its purpose. Categories help maintainers organize how conversations are filed and are customizable to help distinguish categories that are Q&A or more open-ended conversations.{% data reusables.discussions.repository-category-limit %}  For more information, see "[About discussions](/discussions/collaborating-with-your-community-using-discussions/about-discussions#about-categories-and-formats-for-discussions)."  ### Default categories  | Category | Purpose | Type | | :- | :- | :- | | #️⃣ General | Anything and everything relevant to the project | Open-ended discussion | |💡Ideas | Ideas to change or improve the project | Open-ended discussion | | 🙏 Q&A | Questions for the community to answer, with a question/answer format | Question and Answer | | 🙌 Show and tell | Creations, experiments, or tests relevant to the project | Open-ended discussion |  ### Creating a category  {% data reusables.repositories.navigate-to-repo %} {% data reusables.discussions.discussions-tab %} {% data reusables.discussions.edit-categories %} 1. Click **Create**.   !["Create" button for new category](/assets/images/help/discussions/new-category-click-create-button.png)  ### Editing a category  You can edit a category to change the category's emoji, title, description, and discussion format.  {% data reusables.repositories.navigate-to-repo %} {% data reusables.discussions.discussions-tab %} 1.
